**Surah 25: Al-Furqan** is Meccan, except verses 68, 69 and 70, which are Medinan. Its verses number 77.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan)﴾. *Al-barakah* (blessing) means growth and increase, whether sensory or spiritual, and also abundance of good and its permanence. Ascribing it to God, exalted and majestic, in the first sense is the most fitting to the context, since He is exalted above all else in His essence, attributes and acts. Among His acts is the sending down of the noble, inimitable Qur'an, which declares the loftiness of His rank, the sublimity of His attributes, and the foundation of His acts upon wisdom and benefits, free of any flaw whatsoever. The form *tafā'ala* (here *tabāraka*) is used for intensification in what has been mentioned. Forms that cannot literally be ascribed to Him, such as *takabbur* (greatness/pride), are not ascribed to Him, may He be glorified, except in respect of their ultimate purpose. In the second sense, blessing is considered in terms of the abundance of what overflows from Him upon His creatures, especially upon humankind, of all kinds of good, among which is the sending down of the Qur'an, which encompasses all religious and worldly goods. The form then may be used to indicate the growth and increase of those goods, gradually and moment by moment, according to their occurrence or the occurrence of what relates to them. It also serves to indicate, by its independent signification, the ultimate perfection, its actual realisation, and an implication of wonder appropriate to the expression of ultimate glorification. It is not permissible to use this form in respect of anyone other than God, nor to use other forms of this kind in respect of God.

*Al-Furqan* is a verbal noun from *faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn*, meaning he separated the two things, i.e. distinguished between them. The Qur'an is named thus because of its ultimate function of distinguishing truth from falsehood through its rulings, or the one who is right from the one who is wrong through its inimitability (*i'jaz*), or because it is separated, part from part, in itself or in its sending down.

﴿upon His servant﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ). His being mentioned (ﷺ) with this title is for his honour, and to announce that he (ﷺ) is at the highest rank of servanthood, and to draw attention to the fact that a messenger can only be a servant of the one who sent him, in rebuttal of the Christians (*Nasara*).

﴿that he may be﴾: this is the ultimate purpose of the sending down, i.e. He sent it down upon him so that he (ﷺ) might be, or so that the Criterion might be, ﴿a warner to the worlds﴾ of the two species (humans and jinn, *al-thaqalan*), ﴿a warner﴾, i.e. one who warns, or warning in intensive form, or so that its sending down might be a warning, or without mentioning glad tidings, because the discourse is oriented towards the states of the disbelievers. The placement of the preposition *li* before its governing element is for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*). The presentation of "sending down" with respect to "Criterion" in the position of the relative clause (*sila*), which should be known as established to the hearer for the relative pronoun, even though the disbelievers deny it, is to treat it as a known and accepted matter. This indicates the full strength of its proofs and that it is such that hardly anyone could be ignorant of it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾.

(p-201) ﴿Who has the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, dominion belongs to Him alone, to the exclusion of anyone else, neither independently nor shared. It belongs to Him through the overpowering authority and the all-prevailing mastery over both, which entail complete power and total disposal over them and over what is in them: bringing into being and annihilating, giving life and causing death, commanding and forbidding, as His will requires, a will founded on wisdom and benefit. Its place in the grammar is the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, so that the sentence is a resumed clause confirming what came before. Alternatively, it is an attribute of the first relative pronoun, or an explanation of it, or a substitute for it. What lies between them is not foreign, since it is part of the completion of the relative clause (ṣila), and its content is known to the disbelievers beyond any doubt, as in His saying: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?" They will say: "To Allah."﴾ and similar verses. Or it is a praise of Him, exalted is He, in the nominative or the accusative.

﴿and has not taken a son﴾: as those claim who say about the Messiah and the angels what they say. Exalted is Allah above what they describe. This clause is coordinated with the preceding nominal clause of the relative clause, and its placement within the relative clause's chain serves to indicate that its content is so clear and manifest that hardly anyone ignorant could be unaware of it, especially after the preceding statement has been established.

﴿and has had no partner in the dominion﴾: that is, in the dominion of the heavens and the earth. This too is coordinated with the relative clause. Its mention separately, although the exclusive ownership of both by Him, exalted is He, already entails it, is to state explicitly the falsehood of the claim of the Dualists (al-thanawiyya), who assert a plurality of gods and "ward off" [evil] from their own breasts. The placing of the negation of having a son between these two statements serves to draw attention to its independence and its being a principal matter, and to guard against the supposition that it is a completion of the first.

﴿and created everything﴾: that is, He brought into existence every existing thing in a creation proceeding according to a measured order, as His will, founded on profound wisdom, required, such that He created each of them from specific materials, in particular forms, and set within it faculties and properties of differing effects and rulings. 

﴿and then determined it﴾: that is, He prepared it for what He willed for it of properties and actions fitting to it.

﴿with a determination﴾: an unprecedented determination whose measure cannot be grasped and whose essence cannot be reached, such as the disposition of man for understanding, perception, reflection, and contemplation of the affairs of this life and the Hereafter, and for devising varied crafts and practising diverse works; and likewise the conditions of all other kinds. It has been said: by "creation" is meant simply bringing into being and originating, figuratively (majāz), without regard to the sense of determination, though that sense is not absent in reality. The meaning then is: He brought everything into being and determined it in that bringing into being with a determination. As for what has been said, that He named His originating "creation" because He, exalted is He, originates nothing except in a determined manner without disparity, then in it is the point that resorting to figurative usage by applying "creation" to mere origination, stripping it of the sense of determination, and then taking determination into account in any way, is definitively damaging to the intended meaning. It has also been said: the intended sense of the second "determination" is determination for remaining until a specified term. Whichever is the case, the clause functions as a causal explanation (ta'līl) of what precedes it of the clauses comprised in the relative clause, since His creation of all things in that wondrous pattern, just as it requires His exclusive self-sufficiency by His being characterized by the attributes of divinity, requires that everything other than Him, whatever it may be, be contained under His overpowering sovereignty, such that nothing deviates from it in any way. When this is so, how could it be supposed that He has a son, glory be to Him, or a partner in His dominion?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 3:

﴿And they have taken, besides Him, gods﴾ After He had explained the reality of the Truth at the opening of this noble surah, by mentioning His sending down of the Great Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His Messenger (ﷺ), and by describing Him with the attributes of perfection and declaring Him far exalted above what is unfitting to His majestic dignity, He followed this with a report of the falsehoods of the polytheists concerning the One who sent down (the Criterion), Him (glorified is He), concerning the one sent down (the Criterion), and concerning the one upon whom it was sent down, in that order. And the manifest mention (of the polytheists) rather than the pronoun is to show their falsehood, while the pronoun is used without their having been previously mentioned, because of reliance on what preceded it, namely the denial of a partner concerning them. That is: they have taken for themselves, transgressing beyond God (the One whose great affairs have been mentioned in part, namely the exclusive possession of the heavens and the earth by Him, the negation of offspring and partner from Him, and the creation of all things, and their determination in the most perfect determination), gods.

﴿They create nothing﴾, that is: they are not able to create any thing of things at all, ﴿while they are created﴾, like the rest of created beings. It has been said: they are not able to fabricate anything, while they are themselves fabricated, since their worshippers fabricate them by carving and shaping. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they control not for themselves any harm or benefit﴾ is to explain what was not indicated by what preceded it of the degrees of their incapacity and weakness, for some created beings who are incapable of creating may nevertheless control the repelling of harm and the bringing of benefit in general, such as animals; but these (gods) are not able to exercise any control over any harm so as to repel it from themselves, nor over any benefit so as to bring it to themselves, so how could they control any of these two for others? The mention of harm is placed first because repelling it, although it is more important in itself, is the first and earliest degree of benefit. The specific mention of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they control not death, nor life, nor resurrection﴾, that is: they are not able to exercise control over any of these by causing the living to die and the dead to be brought to life and raised again, after explaining their incapacity regarding what is easier than these matters, namely repelling harm and bringing benefit, in order to state explicitly their incapacity regarding each one of what has been mentioned in detail, and to alert to the fact that the God must be capable of all of that. In this there is also an announcement of the extreme of their ignorance and the feebleness of their minds, as though they were not aware that what has been negated of their gods, of the matters mentioned, is absent, needing explicit statement of that.

He began narrating their falsehoods concerning both the revelation and the one to whom it was revealed, and refuting them. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is either a reference to their extremists in disbelief and insolence, namely al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abd Allah ibn Umayya, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and those who allied with them. It is reported from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that the speaker was Mudar ibn al-Harith, and the plural form is used because the others backed him in this. Or the relative pronoun refers to all of them, and it is placed in the position of their pronoun to censure them through what is contained in the relative clause, and to indicate that what they uttered was great disbelief. The word "this" (hadha) in "this is nothing but" belittles the status of what is pointed to. That is, this is nothing but a lie diverted from its proper course.

﴿They say, "He has invented it."﴾ They mean that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) fabricated it. ﴿And others helped him with it.﴾ That is, helped him in fabricating it. ﴿A different people.﴾ They mean the Jews, by conveying to him the reports of the earlier nations, and he expresses them in his own words. It was also said that they were Jabr and Yasar, who used to make swords in Mecca and recited the Torah and the Gospel. It was also said that it was Abis, and its detailed account has already passed in Surat al-Nahl.

﴿Then they have committed injustice and falsehood.﴾ The word "injustice" (zulman) is in the accusative, governed by "they have come" (ja'u), for "ja'a" and "ataa" are used with the meaning of a verb and so take its government. Alternatively, the preposition has been omitted, meaning "with injustice," as al-Zajjaj said. The nunation (tanwin, the added "n" sound on an indefinite noun) is for magnification, meaning that by what they said they have come with a tremendous and great injustice, whose extent cannot be measured, since they made the pure truth, to which falsehood cannot come from before it or behind it, into a fabricated lie invented by a human being. This is in respect of its refined composition and its surpassing style, such that if mankind and jinn gathered together to match it, they would be unable to produce anything like one of its verses. And it is in respect of its containing hidden wisdoms and rulings that bring about religious and worldly felicity, and matters of the unseen, such that human intellects cannot attain it and human faculties and capacities cannot grasp it.

(p-203) ﴿And falsehood.﴾ That is, a great lie that does not reach its full extent, since they attributed to him (ﷺ) what he is innocent of. The particle "fa" (then) is for ordering what follows upon what precedes, but not on the basis that they are two distinct realities in fact, where one occurs after the other or is caused by it. Rather, the second is in fact identical to the first, and the ordering is only in terms of a conceptual difference. The word "qad" (indeed) is to confirm this meaning, for what they brought of injustice and falsehood is the very thing that was previously described about them. But since it differed from it in concept and was more evidently false, it was ordered upon it with "fa", in the manner of a necessary consequence upon what necessitates it, in order to magnify its matter.

And they said, "Tales of the ancients" ﴿وَقالُوا أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾. After having called the Truth, from which there is no escape, a fabricated lie produced with the help of humans, they explained, according to their corrupt assumption, the manner of that help. *Al-asatir* (fabled tales) is the plural of *usatir* or *ustura*, on the pattern of *uhdutha* (a story or anecdote), and refers to the fanciful tales that earlier generations had written down (*sattarahu*).

﴿اكْتَتَبَها﴾ means that he had them written for himself (*katabaha li-nafsihi*), by way of metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), or that he had them written by another (*istaktabaha*). It has also been read in the passive voice (*ala al-bina' lil-maf'ul*), because he (ﷺ) was unlettered (*ummi*). Its underlying form was *iktatabaha lahu katibun* ("a scribe had them written for him"). The lam was deleted, the verb was made to reach the pronoun, so it became *iktatabaha iyyahu katibun*. Then the agent was deleted because the scientific purpose does not depend on its specific identity, and the verb was made to take the detached pronoun, so it became concealed within it.

﴿فَهِيَ تُمْلى عَلَيْهِ﴾ means: those tales are cast upon him after being written down, so that he may memorize them from the mouths of the one who dictates them to him from that writer, since he is unlettered and cannot receive them by reading. Alternatively, they are dictated to the scribe, on the understanding that the meaning of *iktatabaha* is that he intended its writing or its having been written. The pronoun in the genitive, referring back to him (ﷺ), is used because writing is attributed to him (ﷺ) within the sense of *iktitab*.

﴿بُكْرَةً وأصِيلا﴾ means: constantly, or secretly, before people disperse and when they return to their dwellings. Consider this level of enormous audacity. May Allah destroy them; ﴿أنّى يُؤْفَكُونَ﴾ "how are they turned away?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 6:

﴿Say﴾ as a reply to them and a confirmation of the truth: ﴿He has sent it down, who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth.﴾ He, exalted is He, described Himself by the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge of all things known, both manifest and hidden, to signal that what He has sent down contains secrets folded away from the minds of mankind, together with an allusion to the requital of their crimes, which are recounted and which are among the things He knows. That is, this is not something that is fabricated and invented with the help of a people and the writing of others of fabricated tales and myths of the ancients. Rather, it is a matter from heaven, sent down by Allah, the One from whose knowledge nothing among things escapes, and He has deposited in it the various kinds of wisdom and secrets in a wondrous manner, such that human understandings cannot approach it. He has made you all incapable of matching it by its eloquence and rhetoric, and He has informed you of unseen future matters and hidden affairs which are not reached or comprehended except by the grace of the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. But you have made it a lie, a fabrication, of the kind of myths, and by that you have deserved that the whip of punishment be poured down upon you in full.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ it is the reason for what is witnessed of the delay of punishment. That is, He, exalted is He, is eternally and everlastingly constant in forgiveness and mercy, which entail the delay; therefore He does not hasten punishment upon you for what you say concerning His right, despite your full deserving of it and His complete power over it, exalted is He.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 7:

﴿And they say, "What is this Messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ This begins the account of their offence concerning the particular quality of the one to whom it was sent down. The "mā" (what) is interrogative, meaning denial of occurrence and negation; it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), its predicate being what follows it, the prepositional phrase. In this there is a belittling of his status (ﷺ), and calling him (ﷺ) a "Messenger" is by way of mockery of him (ﷺ), as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿eats food﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Messenger," and its governing element is what governs the prepositional phrase, namely the sense of "being established." That is: what and what cause has come about for this one who claims prophethood, while he eats food as we eat, ﴿and walks in the markets﴾ seeking provision as we do? This is according to directing the denial and negation to the cause alone, while the effect, which is the content of the circumstantial clause, is established, as in His saying: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ and His saying: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not expect dignity from God?﴾ Just as neither the absence of belief nor the absence of hope is a matter that is established, yet its occurrence is denied and deemed unlikely because its cause is absent, rather because the cause of its opposite exists, likewise each of eating and walking is a matter that is established, yet its occurrence is deemed unlikely because its cause is absent, rather because the cause of its absence exists. Except that the deeming unlikely of the effect and the denial and negation of the cause in the case of absence of belief and absence of hope are by way of affirmation, while in the case of eating and walking they are by way of scorn and mockery. For they do not deem these two unlikely nor deny their cause in reality; rather they acknowledge their existence and the establishment of their causes. What they deem unlikely is the prophethood that is incompatible with them according to their claim, meaning: if what he claims is true, then why has his condition not differed from ours? And this is nothing but from their bewilderment, the feebleness of their intellects, and the shortness of their vision to sensible things, for the distinguishing of messengers from others is not by corporeal matters but by spiritual matters, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I am only a human like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God.﴾

﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him﴾ i.e., in his form and appearance, ﴿so that he might be a warner along with him﴾: a descent from them from the suggestion that he be an angel free from the need of eating and drinking to the suggestion that an angel be with him to confirm him, to be a support for him in warning, to explain what he says and to clarify it to the common folk.

And His saying, Most High: ﴿Or a treasure is thrown down to him﴾ descends from that rank to the suggestion that a treasure be cast down to him from heaven, on which he could rely, so that he would not need to seek a livelihood, and which would serve as a proof of his truthfulness. And His saying, Most High: ﴿Or he has a garden from which he eats﴾ descends from that to the suggestion of something easier and nearer to occurring. It was also read as "نَأْكُلُ" (*na'kulu*, "we eat") with the *nun al-hikaya* (the nun of quoted speech, in which the speaker's words are reported in the first person plural), and in this there is additional obstinacy and extreme arbitrariness.

﴿And the wrongdoers said﴾: they are the earlier sayers. The apparent noun was used in place of their pronoun in order to record upon them the wrongdoing and transgression of bounds in what they said, since it is a misguidance that exceeds the limits of misguidance, along with what it contains of attributing to him (ﷺ) being bewitched. That is: they said to the believers, ﴿If you follow﴾, i.e., you do not follow, ﴿except a man bewitched﴾, who has been bewitched so that his intellect has been overcome. It was also said: one who has *sihr* (the condition of being bewitched), which is "الرَّئَّةُ" (*al-ri'a*, the windpipe or lungs, here meaning a human being who breathes), i.e., a human and not an angel, the description being for added emphasis. The first is more fitting to their state.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 9:

﴿Behold how they strike similitudes for you,﴾ an expression of amazement at the falsehoods which they have dared to utter, and a marvelling at them. That is: Behold how they have said about you those wondrous sayings, which lie outside the bounds of reason, and which, by reason of their strangeness, have become like proverbs; and how they have invented for you those singular attributes and conditions, far removed from actual occurrence.

﴿So they have gone astray﴾ — that is, from the path of argument, in that they have not produced anything that could proceed from one possessed of even minimal intellect and discernment, so they remain bewildered. (p-205)

﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ — to impugn your prophethood by finding a statement on which they can settle, even if it is false in itself. Or it means: they have strayed from the truth into manifest error, so they find no path leading to it, for whoever is accustomed to employing such falsehoods scarcely comes to be guided to the use of sound premises.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 10:

﴿Blessed is He who﴾ i.e., increased and multiplied is the good of Him who ﴿if He wills, will give you﴾ in this world, speedily, something ﴿better﴾ for you ﴿than that﴾ which they proposed, namely that you should have a garden from which you eat, by hastening for you the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "better" and confirms its superiority over what they said, because that was unrestricted regarding the condition of plurality and the flowing of rivers.

﴿and will give you palaces﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the place (mahall) of the conditional response (jaza'), which is "will make" (ja'l). It was also read in the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction upon itself, because when the conditional verb is in the past tense, its response may be in the nominative or the jussive, as in the words of the poet:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of asking, he says: 'My wealth is not absent, nor is my family [lacking]'."

It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause (isti'naf), announcing what will be his in the Hereafter. It was also read in the accusative (nasb), on the basis that it is a response with a waw (conjunction), and the linking of that to His will, exalted is He, is to indicate that the non-granting of it is by His will, which is founded upon wisdoms and interests. The non-addressing of the answer to the first two proposals serves to alert to their going beyond the circle of reason and their being independent of an answer, because their falsehood and their incompatibility with legislative wisdom are evident. What has some validity in general is the last proposal, for it is not wholly incompatible with wisdom, since some of the prophets, peace be upon them, were given, in this world along with prophethood, a great kingdom.

﴿Nay, they denied the Hour.﴾ This is a turning away from rebuking them by recounting their previous transgressions, and a transition to rebuking them by recounting their other transgressions, in order to arrive at explaining the various kinds of punishment that await them in the Hereafter because of these, through His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blazing Fire﴾, and so on. That is: We have prepared for them a great fire, intensely blazing, of such-and-such a nature, because of their denial of it, in keeping with what the sense conveys. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of their pronoun. Or it means: for everyone who denies it, whoever he may be, and they are included among them by primary inclusion (dukhulan awwaliyyan). He placed "the Hour" in the position of its pronoun to intensify the reprehension. The basis for preparing the Blaze for them, even though it is not merely their denial of the Hour but also their denial of everything the noble Shari'ah (sacred law) brought, is that since the Hour was the proximate cause of their entering the Blaze, the causal link of their denying it to their entering it was indicated.

It was also said that this is a conjunction (atf) upon ﴿And they said: "What is this messenger..."﴾, and so on, with the meaning: Nay, they came with something more astonishing than that, in that they denied the Hour and rejected it, while the reality is that We have prepared a blaze for everyone who denies it. Their audacity in denying it, and their lack of fear of the kinds of punishment prepared for whoever denies it, is more astonishing than the previous statement.

It was also said that it is connected to what precedes it, namely the answer based on verification, which indicates the promise of gardens in the Hereafter, coming to show that this does not benefit them nor is it worth anything, in the manner of the saying of one who said:

Turn aside to Nu'm and greet the ruins of the abode;
what do you greet of a mound and stones?

The meaning: they do not believe in the Hour, so how would they be convinced by this answer, and how would they believe that what He promised you in the Hereafter would be hastened? (p-206) It was also said that the meaning is: Nay, they denied it, so their outlook was confined to worldly pleasures, and they thought that honour lies only in wealth, and they made your poverty a pretext for denying you.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿When it sees them﴾ etc., is a qualifier (sifah) of the Blaze (al-sa'ir), meaning: when it appears to them from a distance, as the gaze of a viewer reaches across a distance. Compare his saying ﷺ: "Their fires should not see each other" (ﷺ), meaning they should not be so close that one of them is within sight of the other, figuratively (majaz), as though some of it sees the rest. The attribution of seeing to it, rather than to them, signals that the raging and roaring come from it, because its anger against them surges upon seeing them, whether literally or figuratively.

The "min" in his saying ﴿from a distant place﴾ indicates that the distance between it and them at the moment it sees them lies beyond the usual limits of distance in familiar journeys, and this adds further to the terror of its condition. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: "From a journey of a year." It was said: "From a journey of a hundred years."

﴿They hear from it raging and roaring﴾: that is, the sound of rage, likening the sound of its boiling to the sound of one enraged and his roaring, which is a sound heard from within his inner body. That said, since life was not conditioned for us by physical structure, it is possible for God the Exalted to create life in it, so that it sees, rages and roars. It was also said that this belongs to its guardians (zabaniyah), and so it is attributed to it by omitting the modified noun (hadhf al-mudaf).

﴿Wa-idhā ulqū minhā makānan﴾ is in the accusative of place (*ẓarf*, an adverbial accusative indicating place), and "minhā" is a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) relating to it, because it was originally a qualifier of it.

﴿Ḍayyiqan﴾ is a qualifier of *makānan* that conveys intensified severity, for distress is with constriction just as ease is with spaciousness. This is the reason Paradise is described as having a breadth of "the heavens and the earth." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Hell will constrict around them as the butt of a spear constricts around the shaft. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about this and said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will be forced into the Fire as a stake is forced into a wall." Al-Kalbī said: "The lower ones are lifted up by the flame, while the upper ones are pressed down by those entering, so they crowd together within it." It is also read as "ḍayqan" with the *yāʾ* silent.

﴿Muqarranīn﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) from the object of *ulqū*, meaning: when they are cast into it, a narrow place, while they are bound together, their hands having been tied to their necks with chains. It was also said: "bound together" means bound with the devils in the shackles, each disbeliever with a devil, and their feet are in fetters (*aṣfād*).

﴿Daʿaw hunālika﴾ means: in that terrifying place and that dreadful condition, ﴿thubūran﴾, that is, they will wish for destruction and cry out, "Woe to us!" (*yā thubūrāh*), [and it will be said to them], "Come, for this is your time and your moment."

﴿Do not call out for one destruction today﴾. This is on the basis of a speech (qawl) being presumed. It is either an accusative (manṣūb) that is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "da'aw" (they called out), meaning: call out to it as something said to them, truly deserving that the angels address them with it, to alert them to the eternity of their punishment, and that they will not be answered in what they call for, nor attain the saving destruction they wish for. Or it is a figurative depiction (tamthīl wa-taṣwīr) of their state by the state of one to whom that is said without any speech or address actually taking place, meaning: call out to it while being worthy of having that said to them. Or it is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnaf) that came as an answer to a question implied by the discourse, as if it were said: "What will happen when they call out as mentioned?" So it is said: "That will be said to them," to dishearten them from what they have set their hopes on of destruction, and to alert them that their punishment, which compels them to seek destruction entirely, is everlasting and has no escape for them. That is: (p-207) do not limit yourselves to one call of destruction.

﴿And call out for many destructions﴾. That is, according to the multiplicity of the calls connected to it, not according to its multiplicity in itself. For what they call for is one destruction in its own right, but whenever a call from those many calls is connected to it, it becomes as though it were a destruction distinct from that to which another call is connected. Its realization is: do not call for it with one call, but call for it with many calls. For what you are in of punishment, by reason of its extreme severity and long duration, requires repeating the call at every moment. This shows the horror and dread of the punishment more clearly than making the multiplicity and renewal of the call due to the multiplicity of the punishment through the multiplicity of its kinds and varieties, or due to its multiplicity through the renewal of the skins, as is not hidden. As for what is said, that the meaning is: "You have fallen into a state in which your destruction is not one but is many," either because punishment has kinds and varieties, each of which is a destruction by its severity and dreadfulness, or because whenever their skins are cooked through they are replaced with others, so there is no end to their destruction, this does not fit the context. How could it, when they are only calling for a destruction that would end their punishment and rescue them from it? So the answer must be a dishearteners of them from that, by showing its impossibility and the permanence of what requires them to seek it, namely the severe punishment. The restriction of the prohibition and the command to "today" is for greater awe and horror, and to alert that it is not like the other familiar days.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 15:

﴿Say﴾ in rebuke of them, in mockery of them, and in regret over what they have missed. ﴿Is that better?﴾ This is a reference to the Blaze (al-sa'ir) that was mentioned, considered in terms of its being described by the terrifying conditions that were detailed; and the sense of distance in the demonstrative is to indicate that it is at the farthest extreme of terror and horror. That is: say to them, "Is that which was mentioned of the Blaze, which I have prepared for those who denied the Hour, whose state is thus and so, and whose people's state is such and such, better?"

﴿or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. That is: which the God-fearing have been promised. The addition of "Garden" to "Eternity" is for praise; it was also said that it is to distinguish it from the gardens of this world. By "the God-fearing" is meant those characterised by taqwa in its absolute sense, not only by the second or third of its degrees.

﴿It shall be﴾ that Garden ﴿for them﴾ in the knowledge of God Most High, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or because what God Most High has promised is certainly to be, so its realisation and occurrence are narrated as already accomplished, ﴿as a recompense﴾ for their deeds, in accordance with the gracious promise that has passed, ﴿and a destination﴾ to which they will return.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 16:**

﴿For them therein is whatever they will﴾. That is, whatever they desire of the varieties of delights, the things they crave, and the kinds of bliss, as in His Exalted words: ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾. Perhaps each group among them is content with what has been granted to them of the degrees of bliss, and the necks of their aspirations do not stretch toward what is above that of the lofty ranks. Thus there is no necessity of deprivation, nor are the ranks of the people of the Gardens made equal.

﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) from the concealed pronoun (*ḍamīr mustatir*) in the prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa-al-majrūr*), because it depends on the subject (*mubtada'*). It is said that it is from the subject of "they will" (*yashā'ūn*).

﴿it was﴾, that is, what they will. It is said that it refers to the promise implied by His Exalted words: ﴿The God-fearing have been promised﴾.

﴿a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one to be asked for﴾. That is, a promise truly promised, such that it is requested and sought, because it is among the things that those who strive for excellence vie for. Or it is "one to be asked for" in the sense that people ask for it in their supplications by saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, or the angels ask for it by saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them﴾. The sense of obligation (*wujūb*) in "upon" (*'alā*) is because the non-fulfilment of His Exalted promise is impossible, and this does not entail that He is compelled to carry it out. For the attachment of His will to the promised thing precedes the promise that necessitates its fulfilment. In mentioning the title of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is an honouring of him (ﷺ), and an indication that he (ﷺ) is the one who attains, the most favoured one to receive the bounties of the noble promise, which is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 17:

(p-208) ﴿And [remember] the Day when He gathers them﴾ is in the accusative case as an object of a hidden, preceding verb, coordinated with His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿"Is that better?"﴾ ..., etc. That is: and mention to them, after the reproach and the regret, the Day when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gathers them. The linking of the reminder to the Day, although the intended meaning is reminding them of the awesome events that occur therein, has had its aspect explained more than once. Or it is in the accusative as an adverb of time of a hidden, subsequent verb, which has been omitted to alert to the completeness of its terror and the enormity of what occurs in it, and to signal that expression falls short of explaining it; that is: on the Day when He gathers them there will be, of the states and terrors, what speech cannot fully express. It is also read with the nun of majesty, by way of iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person, and with a kasra on the shin.

﴿And what they worship besides Allah﴾ is intended to cover both rational beings and others, either because the word "ma" is laid down for all, as indicated by your saying, when you see a figure from afar: "What is it?"; or because what is meant is the attribute and not the essence, as if it were said: "and their objects of worship"; or by giving precedence to the idols over others, alerting that they are like them in falling from the rank of deserving worship; or in consideration of the prevalence of their worshippers. Or what is meant is the angels, the Messiah and 'Uzayr, by the indication of the question and answer; or the idols, whom Allah causes to speak; or they are made to speak by the tongue of the state, as has been said regarding the testimony of the hands and feet.

﴿Then He will say﴾ i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the worshipped ones, after the gathering of all, as a reproach to the worshippers and a rebuke to them. It is also read with the nun, as what is coordinated with it, and this is read with the ya', while the first with the nun, by way of iltifat to the third person.

﴿"Did you lead these My servants astray,﴾ by calling them to your worship, as in His saying: ﴿"Did you say to the people: take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾

﴿"Or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ i.e., from the way by themselves, due to their neglect of correct reflection and their turning away from the guide. So the preposition is dropped and the verb is made to reach the object, as in His saying: ﴿"And He guides to the way"﴾; the original is "to the way" or "for the way". The placing of the two pronouns before the two verbs is because the intended subject of the question is the one who undertakes the action, not the action itself.

[Qalu] This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narration of the question, as if it were said: "What did they reply?" So it was said: they said, [Subhanaka] "Glory be to You," in amazement at what was said to them, because they are either angels, who are infallible, and inanimate objects that have no power over anything; or as an indication that they are the ones marked by glorifying Him, exalted is He, and affirming His oneness, so how could the misguiding of His servants proceed from them; or as a declaration of His transcendence, exalted is He, above rivals.

[Ma kana yanbaghi lana] That is: it was not valid nor proper for us [an nattakhidha min dunika] that we take, i.e., passing beyond You, [min awliya'] any allies, whom we would worship, because of the state we are in, which is incompatible with that. How then could it be conceived that we would cause others to take an ally other than You, let alone that they would take us as an ally, or that we would take allies apart from You; i.e., followers. For the word wali (ally) is applied both to the one followed and to the follower, just as mawla is applied to both the superior and the inferior. From this usage is "the allies of Satan," i.e., his followers. It has also been read in the passive form, from the verb that is transitive to two objects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God took Abraham as a close friend﴾, and its second object is [min awliya'] "some allies," with "min" being partitive, i.e., that we take some allies. According to the first reading, it is superfluous. The indefiniteness of "awliya'" is because they are specific allies, namely the jinn and the idols.

[Wa lakin matta'tahum wa aba'ahum] This is a corrective statement intended to clarify that they themselves were the misguided ones, after the clarification of their exemption from misguiding them. Their evil conduct has been censured, since they made the means of guidance into means of misguidance. That is: we did not misguide them, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment with kinds of blessings so that they would recognize its due and be grateful for it, but they became immersed in desires and plunged into them [hatta nasu al-dhikr] "until they forgot the remembrance," i.e., they became heedless of Your remembrance, or of reflecting on Your bounties and pondering Your signs, so by their evil choice they made the means of guidance a pretext for error.

[Wa kanu] That is: in Your decree, which is founded upon Your eternal knowledge concerning what will proceed from them, regarding the evil deeds they continually choose, [qawman bura] "a people doomed," i.e., perishing. The word "bura" is either a verbal noun described as the agent for emphasis, which is why it is the same for singular and plural; or it is the plural of ba'ir, like 'uwadh is the plural of 'a'idh. The clause is a parenthetical concluding statement affirming the meaning of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they have denied you﴾ is a report of His, the Exalted's, argument against the worshippers, by way of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab), and diverting it away from the objects of worship once their answer is complete and directing it to the worshippers, as an intensification of rebuke and reproach. This is on the assumption of a statement that follows the answer; that is, the Exalted God then says: "So the objects of worship have denied you, O disbelievers, ﴿in what you say﴾," that is, in your saying that they are gods. It has also been said: in your saying, "These misled us." This is rejected by the fact that their denial in this statement has no connection with what follows, namely their inability to turn away (the punishment) or to give victory at all. What follows from it is rather their denial in their claim that they are their gods and their helpers. In any case, the ba' (in bima) means "fi" (in), or it is connected to the denial, with the prepositional phrase being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the object pronoun. It was also read with the ya' (yukadhdhibukum), meaning: they denied you with their saying, "Glory be to You..." (the verse).

﴿So you are not able﴾, that is, you do not possess ﴿turning away﴾, that is, repelling the punishment from you in any way, as indicated by the indefiniteness of the word (in the Arabic), that is, neither directly nor through an intermediary. It has also been said: a stratagem, from their saying, "He manages his affairs (yatasarrafu)," that is, he devises and manages cleverly. It has also been said: repentance.

﴿Nor help﴾, that is, a single instance of help, neither from yourselves nor from others. The fa' is for the sequencing of the inability upon what precedes it, namely the denial. But not in the sense that, had it not been for this, the ability would have actually existed; rather, it is in their claim, since they used to claim that they repel punishment from them and help them. There is in this a form of mockery of them. It was also read: "yastatī'ūn" in the third-person form, meaning: your gods are not able to turn away the punishment from you or devise for you, nor to help you, and what follows the fa' is ordered upon what precedes it, as its explanation has already passed.

﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾, O accountable ones, like the habit of these people, who mounted the back of obstinacy and stubbornness, persisted in their corruption, and exceeded every customary limit in contention ﴿We will make him taste﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿a great punishment﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated, which is the punishment of the Fire. It was also read: "yudhiqhu" (with the pronoun referring to God, glory be to Him, and the Exalted). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun of the verb in the conditional clause. The generality of wrongdoing does not necessitate that the sinner shares with the disbeliever in tasting the great punishment, for the condition in the requirement of the consequence is, by consensus, restricted to the absence of an impediment, and that impediment is repentance; and by consensus, annulment by obedience, and according to us, annulment by pardon.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 20:

(p-210) ﴿Never did We send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ This is an answer to their saying: ﴿What kind of messenger is this, who eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ The clause that follows "illa" (except) is a qualifying description (sifah) of a noun that has been omitted, the omission being safe because the prepositional phrase indicates it, and the clause has been put in its place, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station.﴾ The meaning is: We did not send anyone before you among the messengers except that they were eating and walking. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal), and the implied sense is: except while they eat... etc. It is also read "yamshuna" in the passive voice, meaning: their needs make them walk, or people make them walk.

﴿And We have made some of you﴾ is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), generalizing it to all the messengers, peace be upon them, by way of prominence (taghlib). The intended "some" here are the disbelievers of the nations, for their being singled out for the messengers and following them justifies counting them as a part of them, and by what is in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for some~﴾ their messengers. But not in the sense that We made the whole of the first part ﴿a trial~﴾, that is, a test and an ordeal, for the whole of the second part, nor in the sense that We made an undefined part of the first a trial for an undefined part of the second, since the totality of the messengers, as a totality, is not tested by the totality of the nations, nor is each individual of them tested by each individual of the nations, nor is an undefined part of the first tested by some undefined part of the latter. Rather, the meaning is: We made each specific part of the nations a trial for a specific part of the messengers, as if it were said: And We made each particular nation among the disbelieving nations a trial for its specific messenger who was sent to it. It was not stated explicitly, relying on the testimony of the situation. This is the case. As for generalizing the address to all the accountable (mukallafin) and leaving "some" in its generality and indefiniteness, in the sense of: And We made some of you, O people, a trial for some other of you, this is rejected.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ is the endpoint of the stated making, and it is clear that the trial of each individual of ordinary people is not conditioned on patience, but on what suits his state. Moreover, restricting the mention to this alone, without reference to a counterpart that indicates it, shows that what is fitting for the state of those tested, and what is expected from them, is patience alone. So the intended people must be the messengers, whereby the Prophet ﷺ is consoled. The meaning is: by the necessity of Our wisdom, Our custom has run to test the messengers through their peoples, through their opposition to them with enmity, their harming of them, and their words that go beyond the bounds of fairness, so that you may be patient in the manner of [the messengers'] patience.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ is a noble promise to the Messenger ﷺ of a great reward for his beautiful patience, along with an extra honour for him ﷺ through the turn to the name of the Lord, joined to his pronoun ﷺ.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 21:

﴿And those who do not hope for meeting Us said﴾ This begins the relating of another part of their false sayings and the explanation of their falsehood, following the refutation of their earlier fallacies. The sentence is conjoined with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "What is this Messenger..."﴾ etc. Placing the relative pronoun in the position of the personal pronoun serves to draw attention to what is contained in the relative clause (ṣila), namely that what is related of them is of such atrocity that it would not proceed from one who believes in the return to Allah, exalted and majestic is He. (p-211) The "meeting" (liqa') of a thing is an expression for encountering it without any obstacle preventing its perception in any way. The meaning of meeting Him, exalted is He, is either returning to Him through resurrection and gathering, or meeting His reckoning, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾. By their not hoping for it is meant that they do not expect it at all, since they completely deny resurrection and reckoning, not that they lack hope of a good meeting or lack fear of an evil meeting, for the absence of these two does not entail what they are upon of arrogance, haughtiness, and outright denial of resurrection and reckoning. That is: "And those who do not expect to return to Us, or to Our reckoning which leads to the evil punishment that their saying deserves, said."

﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us?﴾ That is: why were they not sent down to us to inform us of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ)? It is also said: why were they not sent down to us as messengers? This is more fitting in light of their saying: ﴿Or we see our Lord﴾, insofar as both statements arise from the utmost extremity of their obstinate defiance and rebellion, as indicated by His saying: ﴿They have certainly become arrogant within themselves﴾, that is, concerning themselves, to the point that they dared to utter such a monstrous and abominable thing.

﴿And they have transgressed﴾, that is, they have exceeded the bounds in wrongdoing and insolence ﴿with great transgression﴾, reaching its utmost extreme, in that they hoped to attain the rank of direct divine address without the mediation of a messenger or an angel, as they said: ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾ And they were not content with the overpowering miracles they witnessed, before which the deaf mountains would prostrate, but went in their demands every way, until their wicked selves conjured up wishes that the eyes of nations scarcely glance toward, and the necks of resolve do not stretch toward, and which none attains except the people of firm resolve among the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. The lam is the answer to an implied oath, that is: "By Allah, they have certainly become arrogant..." etc. In it is a clear indication of the utmost ugliness of their condition, and a hint of wonder at their arrogance and transgression, which is not hidden.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 25, Verse 22**

﴿On the Day they see the angels﴾ is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*) introduced to explain what they will encounter when they witness the angels descending upon them, which they had demanded, after its grandeur has been established, and to show that this will be at the utmost degree of horror. The phrase ﴿On the Day they see﴾ is used rather than "On the Day He sends down the angels" to signal from the outset that their seeing of the angels will not be in the manner of granting their demand, but in another way, one that is not customary. The word "Day" (*yawm*) is in the accusative of time (*zarfiyyah*), governed by what is indicated by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿There will be no good news that Day for the criminals﴾, since it means: the criminals will not be given good news on that Day. The shift to the negation of the genus (*nafy al-jins*) is for the sake of emphasis in negating good news. As for what has been said, that it means: they will be prevented from good news or deprived of it, in order to diminish the matter in a context of dread, this does not hold, for preventing good news and losing it both imply that there is good news which they are prevented from or lose, and how far this is from its complete negation. Since the negation of it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the affirmation of its opposite, just as the negation of love in His statement, "﴿Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾," is a metonymy for hatred and abhorrence, this indicates the affirmation of the warning for them in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by a verb implied, which is emphasized by "good news," with "lā" not being a negation of the genus. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an object governed by a hidden verb placed before it, meaning: "Remember the Day of their seeing the angels." In any case, "On that Day" (*yawma'idhin*) is a repetition for emphasis and dread, along with what it conveys of the fact that the fronting of the adverbial is for emphasis, not for restricting the negation of good news to that time alone, since that would undermine the portrayal of their condition. The phrase ﴿for the criminals﴾ is an explanation (*tabyin*), in that it is an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun, to record them as criminals together with their disbelief. Taking it in its general sense, so that it includes the sinful believers, and then resorting to the exclusion of them from total deprivation by saying that the negation of good news at that time does not necessitate its negation at all times, so that they may be given good news of pardon and intercession at another time, is far from the truth.

﴿And they will say﴾ is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the negated verb mentioned, which indicates the complete grievousness of the evil that will befall them and the extreme terror of its onset, by explaining that they will say, upon seeing it: ﴿Hijran mahjuran﴾. This is a phrase they utter upon encountering a vengeful enemy or the assault of a terrible calamity, which they use as a plea for protection, asking Allah, exalted is He, to prevent the harm so that it does not reach them. The meaning is as if they were saying: "We ask Allah, exalted is He, to prevent that with a complete prevention and to block it with a full blocking." The vowelling of the *ḥā'* with a kasra (*ḥijr*) is an inflectional variant (*taṣarruf*) of it, as it is restricted to one context, as in *qi'dak* and *'amrak* (where the original forms are used only in fixed expressions). It has been read as *ḥujran* with a *ḍammah*. The meaning is that they seek the descent of the angels, peace be upon them, and demand it, yet when they see them they will dislike meeting them with the utmost dislike, and will be terrified of them with intense terror, and will say what they used to say upon the occurrence of a shameful disaster and the arrival of a dreadful, severe calamity. The word *maḥjūran* is an adjective (*ṣifah*) of *ḥijran*, and it is used for emphasis, as they say: "a dragging train that drags" (*dhayl dhā'il*) and "a very dark night" (*layl alyal*). It has also been said that the angels will say it to despair the disbelievers, in the sense of "forbidden, prohibited for you," meaning forgiveness, or Paradise, or good news, that is, Allah has made that forbidden for you. But this is not clear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 23:

﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds, and make them scattered dust.﴾ This is an explanation of the state of what they used to do in the world: maintaining ties of kinship (sila rahim), relieving the distressed (ighathat malhuf), hospitality to guests (qira dayf), showing grace to a captive (man 'ala asir), and other noble and good deeds of theirs which, had they performed them together with faith, they would have obtained their reward for. The state of them and the state of their deeds mentioned is depicted by the state of a people who opposed their ruler and disobeyed him, so he turned to their possessions and targeted what was in their hands, destroying them by ruin and burning and tearing them apart completely, such that he left neither trace nor remnant of them. That is: We intended them and nullified them, meaning We made their invalidity manifest entirely, without there being any turning or anything to which their likeness is intended to be compared.

Al-habaʾ (هَباء): something like dust seen in the rays of the sun entering through a window, from al-habwa (هَبْوَة), which is dust. "Manthuran" (مَنثُورًا) is its attribute; by it their deeds that were rendered void are likened in their insignificance and uselessness, and then to what is scattered from it in its dispersal such that it cannot be gathered. Alternatively, it is a third object (maf'ul thalith) insofar as it is like a predicate after a predicate, as in His exalted saying: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 24:

﴿Ashab al-Jannah (the companions of the Garden)﴾ refers to the believers indicated in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of eternity which has been promised to the God-fearing...?"﴾ and so on.

﴿Yawma'idhin (on that day)﴾ means: on the day when what has been mentioned will occur, namely the absence of good tidings, their saying "a forbidding, forbidden [barrier]," and the making of their deeds into scattered dust.

﴿Khayrun mustaqarran (better in resting-place)﴾: al-mustaqarr is the place in which one settles for most of the time, for sitting together and conversing.

﴿Wa ahsanu maqilan (and better in place of noontime rest)﴾: al-maqil is the place to which one retreats for rest and for enjoying the company of spouses and dalliance with them. It was so named because enjoyment in it generally occurs at the time of the qayluleh (midday rest). It has also been said that it is so named because the reckoning is concluded at the middle of that day, so the people of the Garden take their midday rest in the Garden and the people of the Fire in the Fire. The attribution to it of added beauty, together with the fact that it is better, through its being coordinated with the resting-place, is a symbol that it is adorned with every kind of ornament and embellishment. The preference (tafdil) considered in both of these may be either for the intensification of the quality without restriction, meaning that they are at the utmost degree of excellence of resting-place and beauty of noontime rest, or in comparison to what the disbelieving affluent had in the world, or to what they have in the Hereafter, in a mocking manner toward them, as has passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Say: 'Is that better..."﴾ the verse. Furthermore, it has been permitted that one of the two be understood as the verbal noun or as time, indicating that their place and their time are the most pleasant that can be imagined of places and times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 25:

(p-213) ﴿And the day the heaven is split asunder﴾ i.e., it opens up. Its original form is "tatashaqqaqu" (تَتَشَقَّقُ), with one of the two tā' letters elided, as in "talaẓẓā" (تَلَظّى). It is also read with the tā' assimilated into the shīn (idgham, assimilation of letters).

﴿with the clouds﴾ because of the emergence of clouds from it, namely the clouds mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await aught but that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud, and the angels?﴾ It has been said: it is a white, thin cloud, like mist; it was not granted except to the Children of Israel.

﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descending﴾ i.e., a descent that is wondrous and unlike what is customary. It has been said: the heaven will be split heaven by heaven, and the angels will descend through that cloud bearing the scrolls of the deeds of the servants. It has also been read as "wa-nazalati al-malā'ikatu" (وَنَزَلَتِ المَلائِكَةُ), "wa-nunzilu" (وَنُنْـزِلُ) and "wa-nunazzilu" (وَنُنَـزِّلُ) in the first-person plural form of inzal (إنزال, causing to descend) and tanzil (تنزيل, sending down in stages), "wa-nazzala al-malā'ikata" (وَنَزَّلَ المَلائِكَةَ), "wa-anzala al-malā'ikata" (وَأنْزَلَ المَلائِكَةَ), and "wa-nazala al-malā'ikatu" (وَنَزَلَ المَلائِكَةُ), with the elision of the nūn, which is the first radical of the verb, from tanazzala (تَنَـزَّلَ).

﴿The sovereignty on that Day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾. That is: the dominion that prevails, the total and general possession, established in form and in meaning, outwardly and inwardly, such that it has no cessation at all, belongs to the Most Merciful on that Day. So "al-mulk" (the sovereignty) is the subject (mubtada'), "al-haqq" (truly) is its qualifier (sifah), "lil-Rahman" (to the Most Merciful) is its predicate (khabar), and "yawma'idhin" (on that Day) is an adverbial complement (zarf) specifying the time when the predicate applies to the subject. The benefit of this restriction is that the sovereignty mentioned belongs to Him, the Exalted, exclusively on that Day, whereas in the other days of this world others also have some nominal disposition. It has been said: "al-mulk" is the subject, "al-haqq" is its predicate, "lil-Rahman" is connected to "al-haqq" or to a deleted element functioning as a clarification (tabyin), or to a deleted element that is a qualifier of "al-haqq", and "yawma'idhin" is an object-complement governed by "al-mulk". It has also been said: the predicate is "yawma'idhin", and "al-haqq" is an adjective (na't) of "al-mulk" and of "lil-Rahman" according to what has been mentioned. In any case, the sentence in its meaning governs the adverbial complement, that is: God, the Exalted, is alone in sovereignty on the Day when the heavens are split open. It has also been said: the adverbial complement is in the accusative governed by what has been mentioned, so the sentence is then a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) introduced to explain His states and terrors. The mention of Him under the title of "al-Rahmaniyyah" (the Most Merciful) serves to indicate that His being characterized by utmost mercy does not lighten the matter for the disbelievers, since they do not deserve mercy, as in His saying: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?﴾. The meaning is: the true sovereignty on that Day belongs to the Most Merciful.

﴿And it was﴾ that Day, even though the sovereignty in it belongs to God, the Exalted, who is abundant in mercy to His servants, ﴿a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, severe for them. The fronting of the prepositional phrase ("'ala al-kafirin") is for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil). As for the believers, it will be easy for them by the grace of God, the Exalted. It has come in a hadith: "It will be made easy on the Day of Resurrection for the believer until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he prayed in the world." The sentence is a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) that confirms what precedes it.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 25, verse 27:

﴿And on the Day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾. Biting the two hands and the fingertips, eating the fingers, gnawing the teeth, and similar acts are kinayat (metonymic expressions) for rage and regret, because they are among its accompaniments. The wrongdoer (al-zalim) here refers either to: "'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, as is said, for he used to frequently sit with the Prophet ﷺ. One day he invited him to his hospitality, but the Prophet ﷺ refused to eat his food until he uttered the two testimonies of faith, so he did. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was his friend, and he rebuked him, saying, 'You have apostatized!' He replied, 'No, but he refused to eat my food while he was in my house, so I felt ashamed before him and bore witness for him.' Ubayy said, 'I will not be satisfied with you unless you go to him, step on his neck, and spit in his face.' He found him prostrating in Dar al-Nadwa and did so. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'I will not meet you outside Makkah except that I will strike your head with the sword.' He was taken captive on the Day of Badr, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) to kill him, and he was killed. It is also said that 'Asim ibn Thabit al-Ansari killed him. The Prophet ﷺ stabbed Ubayy in single combat on the Day of Uhud, and he returned to Makkah and died.'" Or the wrongdoer refers to the category of wrongdoers in general, which includes him as a primary entrant.

And His saying, ﴿saying﴾ and so on, is a hal (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of "yaʿaddu" (bites). His saying, ﴿Oh, woe is me!﴾ and so on, is the quoted speech. The "ya" (oh) is either merely for alerting, without intending to specify whom is alerted, or the addressee is omitted, meaning: "O people, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger." ﴿a way﴾ means one path that saves from these predicaments, which is the path of truth, and I had not been led by the paths of misguidance. Or: "I had found in his companionship ﷺ a path, but I was not astray; I never had a path at all."

O woe is me! The ya of the speaker is replaced by an alif, as in ṣaḥārā and mudārā. It is also read according to the original form, "yā wayelatī" (O my woe!), meaning: my destruction. Come, be present, for this is your time.

"Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend." He means whoever led him astray in the world. Fulān is a kināya (a euphemistic or figurative designation) for proper names, just as al-hana is a kināya for kinds. It is said that fulān is a kināya for the proper name of a rational male, fulāna for that of a rational female, ful is a kināya for an indefinite rational male, and fulla for an indefinite rational female. Al-fulān and al-fulāna are used for non-rational beings. Fulla is specifically used in the vocative, except out of necessity, as in his verse:

"In the heat of the quarrel, hold back so-and-so from such-and-such."

And his verse:

"Take my second edge away from Falan and Fulān."

Ful is not a truncated form (tarkhīm) of fulān, contrary to al-Farrā'. They differed about the lām of ful and fulān: it is said to be a waw, and it is said to be a ya. This is the case. If by the wrongdoer is meant ʿUqba, then fulān is a kināya for Ubayy. If by it is meant the category, then it is a kināya for the proper name of anyone whom he misleads, whoever he may be, from among the devils of mankind and the jinn.

This wish, although it is brought out to display regret and anguish, nevertheless contains a kind of excuse and self-justification, by shifting the blame for his own offence onto another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he led me astray from the Reminder﴾ is an explanation of his aforementioned wish and a clarification of his excuse. Its opening with the oath-particle "lam" (al-lam al-qasamiyyah) serves to emphasize the declaration of his error and to show his remorse and regret. That is: "By God, he indeed led me astray from the remembrance of God Exalted, or from the Qur'an, or from the admonition of the Messenger (ﷺ), or from the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah)."

﴿After it had come to me﴾ and I had come to be firmly established in it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter﴾ means: exceedingly forsaking, in that he allies himself with him until he brings him to destruction, then abandons him and does not benefit him. It is an interjected statement (i'tiraD) confirming the content of what precedes it, either from God Exalted's own speech, or as part of the wrongdoer's speech, in that he named his companion "Satan" after describing him with misguidance, which is the most specific of the satanic attributes; or in that he intended by "Satan" Iblis, because he is the one who prompted him to befriend the misguiders and oppose the Messenger, the guide (ﷺ), through his whispering and seduction. However, describing him with forsaking indicates that he used to promise him in this world and hold out hopes to him that he would benefit him in the Hereafter, and this is more fitting to the condition of Iblis.

﴿And the Messenger said﴾ is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us said…﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) that is brought in to magnify what they said and to show the terrors and calamities that will befall them in the Hereafter. The Prophet (ﷺ) is mentioned here under the title of Messenger in order to establish the truth and to refute them head-on, since what is reported of them amounted to a disparagement of his prophethood (ﷺ). That is, they said such-and-such, and the Messenger, after witnessing from them the utmost rebellion and the extreme of tyranny, complained to his Lord, mighty and majestic, saying: ﴿My Lord, my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned.﴾ (p-215) "My people" means those of whom the shameful things just mentioned were reported. ﴿This Qur'an﴾ includes these verses, which speak of the kinds of punishment that will befall them in the Hereafter, as the demonstrative word indicates.

﴿Abandoned﴾ (mahjūran): that is, it was entirely forsaken. They did not believe in it, did not give it any heed at all, and were not moved by its threats. Within this is an allusion that it is the duty of the believer to attend constantly to the Qur'an, so that he does not fall under the apparent meaning of this noble verse. It is reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever learns the Qur'an and hangs a copy of it but does not attend to it or look into it, will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'O Lord of the worlds, Your servant has taken me as something abandoned; judge between me and him.'" It has also been said that the word is derived from "hajara" meaning to talk nonsense, that is, they made it something of nonsense, either according to their false claim, or by talking nonsense about it when they heard it, as is related of them in their saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise against it.﴾ It is also permissible that mahjūr should mean the same as hajr (nonsense), like majlūd (flogged) and ma'qūl (rational), so the meaning would be: they took it as nonsense and raving. In this there is a warning and a threat that is not hidden, for when the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, complained to God, exalted is He, of their people's speech, He hastened the punishment for them and they were not given respite.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 31:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus have We appointed for every prophet an enemy among the criminals﴾ is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and an encouragement for him to follow the example of the prophets before him, peace be upon them, meaning: just as We have appointed for you enemies among the polytheists, who say what they say and do falsehoods, We have appointed for every prophet among the prophets, who are the bearers of the sharia (sacred law) and those who call to it, an enemy from among the criminals of their people. So be patient as they were patient.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord suffices as a guide and a helper﴾ is a generous promise to him (ﷺ) of guidance to all his objectives and of victory over his enemies, meaning: your Lord, the Master of your affair and the One who brings you to perfection, suffices you as a guide to what brings you to the furthest of ends, of which among its components is the conveying of the Book to its term and the enforcement of its rulings over the necks of the world until the Day of Resurrection, and as a helper for you against all who oppose you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 32:

﴿And those who disbelieve say⦗…⦘﴾ This is a report of their particular proposal concerning the Noble Qur'an, following the report of their proposal concerning him (ﷺ). The ones saying it are the same ones who said it first, and their being mentioned by the title of disbelief serves to censure them and to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him⦗…⦘﴾ The sending down (tanzil) here is free of the meaning of gradualness, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾. It is permissible that it be intended to indicate the great quantity of what was sent down in itself, i.e., "Why was it not all sent down ﴿all at once﴾ like the three Books," and the invalidity of this foolish statement is hardly hidden from anyone. For the earlier Books, the proof of their soundness and the evidence that they were from God, exalted is He, was not their inimitability. As for the Noble Qur'an, the clear proof of its soundness is the sign that it is from God, exalted is He: its inimitable composition, enduring through the ages, realized in every part of it, its parts measured by the length of the shortest surah, according to how the challenge was issued. There is no doubt that what the orbit of inimitability revolves around is conformity to what circumstances require, and from the necessity of their change and renewal comes the necessary change of what conforms to them. Moreover, in it there are many benefits, some of which were pointed to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾. This is a resumptive statement coming from Him, exalted is He, to refute their false claim (p-216) and to explain the wisdom in gradual sending down. The kaf has a place in the accusative as an adjective of an emphatic verbal noun for an implied verb, which is explained by what follows it, and that is a reference to what is understood from their speech, i.e.: "Like that gradual sending down which they disparaged and whose opposite they proposed, We sent it down, not as a different sending down, so that by that gradual sending down We may strengthen your heart. For in it there is ease for memorizing the composition, understanding the meanings, mastering the rulings, and grasping the details of the wisdoms and benefits observed in them, explained according to their occasions, and that they are bound to their causes which called for their legislation at first, or their alteration by abrogation (naskh), from the circumstances of the responsible persons." Likewise, most of what came in the Glorious Qur'an of reports and other matters is connected to events that arise from sayings and deeds, and from the nature of their renewal comes the renewal of what is connected to them, such as the proposals made by the disbelievers, which call for reporting them and refuting them, and explaining what their state will come to in the Hereafter. Moreover, in this proposal they are like one who seeks his own death with his own hoof, since they were commanded to produce the like of one of the installments of the sending down, and so their incapacity to produce a counterpart became evident, and the earth, vast as it is, became constricted for them. How much more so if they were challenged with all of it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We arranged it in arrangement﴾ is coordinated with that implied verb. The indefiniteness of "tartilan" is for magnification, i.e.: "Thus We sent it down and arranged it in a wondrous arrangement whose measure cannot be estimated." The meaning of its arrangement is its division verse after verse, as said by al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "We made it clear with a clarity that contains arrangement and firmness." al-Suddi said: "We detailed it in detail." Mujahid said: "We made some of it follow upon others." It was also said: it is the command to recite it with arrangement, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And recite the Qur'an with measured recitation﴾. And it was said: "We recited it to you through the tongue of Jibril, peace be upon him, little by little, over twenty or twenty-three years, with deliberation and unhurried pace."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 33:**

﴿And they will not bring you any parable﴾ from among the parables, of which part is what is related of their ugly proposals, which lie outside the sphere of sound reason and which, for this purpose, take the place of parables. That is: they will not bring you a strange statement that is a parable in falsehood, by which they intend to discredit you and the Qur'an, ﴿but We have brought you﴾ in opposition to it ﴿the truth﴾, that is, the true answer, firm and established, which overturns it and cuts off the root of the talk and dispute, as has passed of the sound answers that uproot their shameful questions and utterly crush them.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and better explanation﴾, is coordinated with "the truth": that is, We have brought you the best of goodness in itself, not that what they bring has some goodness in general and this is better than it, as has passed.
