The exception is a *istithna' mufarragh* (an exception in which the excluded element is not stated, so the exception is taken from the general sense of the sentence), and its place is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). That is: they will not bring you a parable except at the time of Our bringing you the truth from which there is no turning away. In it there is, by its indication, the implication of hastening to nullify what they brought and of strengthening his heart, peace be upon him, which is not hidden. This, by its express wording, speaks of the falsehood of all the questions and the soundness of all the answers, and by its allusion it indicates the falsehood of the last question and the soundness of its answer, for had the revelation of the Qur'an not been gradual, it would not have been possible to nullify those shameful proposals, nor would the strengthening of his heart, peace be upon him, have been achieved from that aspect.

Moreover, it has been permitted that the *mathal* (parable) be an expression for the Arabic attribute which they used to propose that he (ﷺ) possess: such as having a king accompanying him, being independent of eating and drinking, possessing a treasure and a garden, and the Qur'an being sent down to him all at once. The meaning is: they will not come to you with a strange state which they propose that you be described by, saying, "Why was he not in this state? If not, We would have given him, of the possible states, what in Our wisdom and will it is right for him to be given, and what is better in revealing what he was sent with and in proof of its soundness, namely what you are in essence (p. 217) and attributes." This is rejected by the stated exception, for what is understood from it is that what God, exalted is He, gave him of the truth is consequent upon what they brought of falsehoods, crushing them. There is no doubt that what God, exalted is He, bestowed upon him of noble qualities fitting for prophethood, He gave him from the very beginning, not in response to the proposals reported of them, in order to crush and nullify them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 34:

﴿Those who will be gathered on their faces to Hell﴾. That is: they will be gathered, being on their faces, dragged along on them and pulled toward Hell. It was also said: their faces will be turned over onto their necks and their feet upward. It was narrated from him (ﷺ): ﴿People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in three groups: a third upon mounts, a third upon their faces, and a third upon their feet, walking briskly.﴾ As for what was said, that their hearts are attached to the lowly things and their faces are turned toward them, this is far-fetched, because the terror of that Day is not such that they would retain any attachment to the lowly things or any turning toward them in general. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) may be in the accusative or the nominative in the sense of censure, or in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾, it is a substitute (badal) for it, or an explanatory apposition (bayan) for it. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿worse in place and further astray in way﴾ is its predicate (khabar), or the demonstrative noun is a second subject (mubtada' thani), and "worse" (sharr) is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the relative pronoun. Describing the way (sabil) with straying is a figurative attribution (al-isnad al-majazi) for emphasis. The one being compared against is the Messenger (ﷺ), following the pattern of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry...﴾ It is as if it were said: what drives them to these proposals is belittling his place (ﷺ) by misleading his way, and they do not know their own state, so that they would know that they are worse in place and further astray in way. It was also said that this is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in their abode and finer in their resting place.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 35:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʾnafa*, a clause that begins a new sentence without grammatical dependence on what precedes it), brought in to confirm what has passed of consolation and of the promise of guidance and victory in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord suffices as guide and helper﴾, by relating what occurred between the prophets mentioned, upon them be prayers and peace, and their people, in a summary account that is sufficient for the purpose intended. The *lam* (*lam* of oath) is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, We certainly gave Musa the Torah (*al-Tawrat*)", that is, We sent it down to him, at the same time.

﴿And We made with him﴾: the adverbial complement (*al-zarf*, the adverbial of time or place) is connected to *ja'alna* (we made). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿his brother﴾ is the first direct object of it. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Harun﴾ is either a substitute (*badal*) for "his brother", or an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayan*, an apposition that clarifies the noun it follows) to it, in reverse of what occurred in surah Ta-Ha. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿as a vizier﴾ is the second direct object of it. The meaning of *wazir* has already been explained there. That is: We made him a vizier to him at the outset of the matter.

ي﻿﻿Then We said (to them at that time), "Go to the people who denied Our signs." (The people here were Pharaoh and his folk.) The signs are the nine clear miracles that appeared through the hands of Moses, peace be upon him. The people were not described to them in this manner when they were sent to them, because the denial of the signs came after the manifestation of the signs, which came after their going, which in turn came after the command to go. Rather, they were described this way only in narrating to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as an explanation of the cause of their contempt for what is related afterward of the destruction. That is: "Go to them and show them all Our signs, and they denied them with persistent denial."

Then We destroyed them (﴿فَدَمَّرْناهُمْ﴾) immediately after that persistent denial, a destruction (﴿تَدْمِيرًا﴾) that was wondrous and terrible, whose extent cannot be measured and whose reality cannot be grasped. He limited the account to the two ends of the story, being satisfied with what is the intended point. Interpreting His words, Exalted is He, ﴿فَدَمَّرْناهُمْ﴾ to mean "We decreed their destruction" is an evident distortion with no justification, since there is no beneficial point worth mentioning in relating a decree of destruction that has already occurred and passed. The mention at the opening of the story of giving the Book, although it came after the people's destruction and had no part in their ruin, like the other signs, is to announce from the outset that he (ﷺ) would attain the utmost perfection and reach the ultimate of hopes, which is the rescue of the Children of Israel from the dominion of Pharaoh and guiding them to the right path through the rulings in the Torah. By this, the promise of guidance is confirmed in the manner already explained. It is also recited as "fa-dammartuhum" and "fa-dammarnāhum" with emphasis by the heavy nūn.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 37:

﴿And the people of Noah﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by His words, exalted is He, ﴿then We destroyed them﴾. That is: "And We destroyed the people of Noah." It has also been said that it is conjoined to the object of "then We destroyed them." The sequence of the destruction of these people following what came before it is not a necessary consequence of the destruction of those, especially since its cause has been made clear by His words, exalted is He: ﴿when they denied the Messengers﴾. That is: Noah and those Messengers before him; or Noah alone, because denying him is denying all of them, since they agree on tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and Islam. It has also been said that it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb which is explained by His words, exalted is He: ﴿We drowned them﴾. This is possible only if the word "lamma" (when) is taken as a temporal adverb. But if it is taken as a particle of existence for existence (lamma of causation), then it is not possible, because in that case it has its own response clause, and the response of "lamma" does not explain what precedes it. Moreover, it disrupts the conjunction of the following accusatives to "the people of Noah," since their destruction was not by drowning. So the preferred view is the earlier one. His words, exalted is He, ﴿We drowned them﴾ are a resumptive clause explaining the manner of their destruction.

﴿And We made them﴾ That is: We made their drowning, or their story, ﴿a sign for the people﴾. That is: a great sign by which everyone who witnessed it or heard of it may take a lesson. It is the second object of "We made," and "for the people" is an adverbial complement either attached to the word itself or related to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) modifying "a sign," since if it came after it, it would be an attribute of it.

﴿And We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾ That is: for them. The explicit mention in place of the pronoun is to signal their excess in disbelief and denial.

﴿a painful punishment﴾ This is the punishment of the Hereafter, since there would be no benefit in reporting the habitual punishment which has already been mentioned as having occurred before. Or it refers to all the remaining wrongdoers who did not take heed from what befell those before them, so that the Quraysh enter among them in the first instance. The punishment may be understood as both worldly and otherworldly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 38:

﴿And ʿAd﴾: it is coordinated with "the people of Noah" (qawm Nuh). It has also been said that it is coordinated with the first object of "jaʿalnahum" (We made them). It has also been said that it is coordinated with "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), since the sense is "and We promised the wrongdoers." Both of these are far-fetched.

﴿And Thamud﴾: what is said regarding it and what follows it is the same as what is said regarding what precedes it. It has been read as "wa-Thamudan" (with the accusative ending), either by interpreting the name as referring to the tribe (al-hayy) or on the basis that it is the name of the remote ancestor (al-ab al-aqsa).

﴿And the companions of al-Rass﴾: they are a people who worshipped idols. God Most High sent to them Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, but they denied him. While they were around al-Rass, which is a well that had not been walled up after it collapsed, they were swallowed up by the earth together with their dwellings. It has been said that al-Rass is a village in Falj al-Yamama where there were remnants of Thamud. A prophet was sent to them, but they killed him and were destroyed. It has also been said that it is the trench (al-ukhdud). It has been said that it is a well in Antioch in which they killed Habib al-Najjar. It has also been said that they were the companions of Handhala ibn Safwan, the Prophet (ﷺ), whom God tested with a great bird that had every color, and they named it ʿAnqa' because of the length of its neck. It used to inhabit their mountain, which is called Fakh or Dakh, and it would swoop down on their children and snatch them if hunting became scarce for it (p-219). For this reason it was called Mughrib. Handhala, peace be upon him, invoked God against it, and a thunderbolt struck it. Then they killed him, peace be upon him, and so they were destroyed. It has also been said that they were a people who denied their messenger, so they "rassuhu," that is, they thrust him into a well.

﴿And generations﴾: that is, people of generations. It has been said that a generation (qarn) is forty years, and it has been said seventy, and it has been said one hundred and twenty. ﴿Between those﴾: that is, between those mentioned groups and nations. The speaker may mention various things and then refer to them collectively with "that," and the reckoner may count large numbers and then say, "So-and-so is such-and-such, upon that which was mentioned and that which was counted."

﴿Many﴾: none knows their number except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. Perhaps the brevity in describing the affairs of those generations with this general statement is because each of them was not, in fame and strangeness of story, on the level of the nations mentioned.

[And each] is in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by a suppressed verb (muḍmar) that is indicated by what follows it, since coining parables (ḍarb al-mathal) carries the sense of admonition and warning. The omitted element for which the nunation (tanwīn) compensates refers either to the peoples whose causes of destruction were not mentioned, or to all of them, since what is related about the people of Noah and the people of Pharaoh, namely their denial of the signs and the messengers, is not a lack of effect from the parables that were coined. That is: We reminded and warned each one of those mentioned.

﴿We set forth for him parables﴾, i.e., We made clear to him the wondrous stories that restrain them from the disbelief and sins in which they are, through the messengers.

﴿And each﴾ refers to the hopes, which are the deliverance of the Children of Israel. ﴿We destroyed with a utter destruction﴾, a wondrous and awesome destruction, because they were not affected by that, did not heed it, and persisted in the disbelief and transgression in which they were. The root of al-tatbīr is al-tafttīt (crumbling to pieces). Al-Zajjāj said: Everything that you break and crumble, you have tabbarta it, and from this comes al-tibr, meaning the fragments of gold and silver.

**[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 40]**

﴿And they have certainly passed﴾: this is a resumptive (new) clause, brought to show that they witnessed the traces of the destruction of some of the destroyed nations and did not take warning from them. Its opening with an oath serves to strengthen what it affirms, meaning: by God, the Quraysh have indeed passed by, in their trading journeys, to Syria.

﴿the town that was rained upon﴾: that is, destroyed by stones. These were the towns of the people of Lot. They were five towns, and only one of them was spared, whose people did not commit the wicked deed. As for the rest, God the Exalted destroyed them with stones, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿the rain of evil﴾. Its (*intiṣāb*, grammatical case) may be either an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkid*) with its augmenting elements omitted, as is said in *anbatahu Allāhu nabātan ḥasanan* ("God caused him to grow a good growth"), meaning: the raining of evil; or it may be a second object (*maf'ūl thānin*), since the sense is: "I gave" or "I bestowed the rain of evil."

﴿Did they not used to see it?﴾: this is a rebuke directed at them for neglecting to reflect when witnessing what necessitates it. The interrogative particle (*hamzah*) is for denying the negation of their continuous seeing of it, and for affirming its continuity in accordance with the continuity of what necessitates it, namely their passing by it. It is not for denying the continuity of their not seeing it, and affirming that they did see it in general. The *fā'* (then) is for coordinating what follows it with an implied element required by the context, meaning: did they not look at it, so that they did not see it? Or: did they used to look at it, yet not see it, during their repeated passages, so that they might take warning from what they used to witness of the traces of the punishment? Thus the denial in the first reading is of both not looking and not seeing together, while in the second it is of not seeing despite the realized looking that necessitates it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ is either a turning away (*iḍrāb*) from what precedes it, namely their not seeing the traces of what befell the people of the towns of punishment, and an explanation that their not taking warning was due to their denial that this was a punishment for their sins. It is not because they did not see its traces. Except that it contents itself, instead of explicitly stating their denial of that, with mentioning what it entails of their denial of the otherworldly recompense, which is the ultimate purpose of the creation of the world. This is alluded to by the absence of resurrection, that is, the absence of expecting it. It is as if it were said: Rather, they used to deny the resurrection which entails the otherworldly recompense, and they did not consider any soul to have any resurrection at all, although it is certain to occur and is general for all people, and its occurrence is constant. How, then, would they acknowledge a worldly recompense for a particular group, when there is no regularity or necessary connection between it and sins, so that they might be reminded and take warning from what they witnessed of the traces of destruction? Rather, they attribute it to mere coincidence. Or it is a transition from the rebuke for neglecting to reflect, mentioned above, to a rebuke for something greater than that, namely their not expecting a resurrection.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 41:

﴿وَإذا رَأوْكَ إنْ يَتَّخِذُونَكَ إلا هُزُوًا﴾ i.e., they do not take you except as an object of mockery (مَهْزُوءًا بِهِ), in the sense of restricting (qasr) their treatment of him (ﷺ) to their taking him as a mockery (هُزُؤًا), not in the sense of restricting their taking him to his being a mockery, as is the immediate understanding from the apparent wording. It is as if it were said: "They do not treat you except by taking you as a mockery." Its verification has already been discussed in His words, exalted is He, ﴿I follow only what is revealed to me...﴾ in Surat al-An'am.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾, it is related (مَحْكِيٌّ) after an implied saying (قَوْلٍ مُضْمَرٍ), and it is a circumstantial clause (حالٌ) from the subject of ﴿they take you﴾. That is: they mock you, saying: ﴿"Is this the one who..."﴾ etc. The demonstrative (الإشارَةُ) serves to belittle, and to highlight God's sending of a messenger in the guise of acknowledgment, by making it a relative clause (صِلَةً) for the relative pronoun (الموصول) which is his (ﷺ) attribute, even though they are in extreme denial of his (ﷺ) being sent, by way of sarcasm (التَّهَكُّمِ) and ridicule. Otherwise they would have said: "Has God sent this one as a messenger?" or "Is this the one who claims that God has sent him as a messenger?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 42:

﴿إنْ كادَ﴾ "In" is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of "anna," and the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) is omitted, meaning: "Indeed he nearly..." ﴿لَيُضِلُّنا عَنْ آلِهَتِنا﴾ meaning: he would turn us away from their worship with a complete turning away, such that he would distance us from them altogether, and not merely from their worship. The shift to "misguide" (al-idlal) is for the sake of the extreme of their error, by claiming that worshipping them is a straight path.

﴿لَوْلا أنْ صَبَرْنا عَلَيْها﴾ meaning: we remained steadfast in it and held firmly to its worship. "Lawla" in such expressions functions, in meaning, as a restriction of the absolute judgment, as indicated in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَلَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهِ ...﴾ and so on. This is an acknowledgment from them that he (ﷺ) had reached such a degree of striving in calling to the truth, displaying miracles, establishing proofs and clear evidences, that they nearly abandoned their religion, were it not for the excess of their obstinacy and the extreme of their defiance. It is related that this is a statement of Abu Jahl.

﴿وَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a response from Him, exalted is He, to the end of their speech, and a rejection of what it implies of attributing error to him (ﷺ) within the act of misguiding. That is: they will certainly come to know, though it be delayed, ﴿حِينَ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ﴾ the punishment which their disbelief and defiance necessitate, ﴿مَن أضَلُّ سَبِيلا﴾ "who is further astray in way?" In it is what is not hidden of threat, and an alert that He, exalted is He, does not neglect them, even though He gives them respite.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 43:

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ This is an expression of wonder directed at the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at the abhorrent state of these people, after the recounting of their ugly sayings and deeds (p-221) and the explanation of the destination and final outcome that awaits them, and it is a warning that this matter is so strange that it ought to be seen and wondered at. "Ilahahu" (his god) is the second object of "ittakhadha" (took), placed before the first for the sake of emphasis on it, because it is the element around which the matter of wonder revolves. As for one who imagines that the two are in their natural order, on the basis that both are equal in definiteness, he has erred, for he has overlooked that the second object in this construction is the one qualified by the newly arising state; that is: "Have you seen him who made his desire a god for himself, without any deliberation, and built the affair of his religion upon it, turning away entirely from listening to the dazzling proof and the luminous evidence?" The meaning is: look at him and be amazed at him.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ is a denial and a disavowal of the Prophet (ﷺ) being a watcher over him, restraining him from the error he is in and guiding him to the truth, willingly or unwillingly. The "fa" (then) is for the ordering of the denial upon what precedes it, the state that necessitates it; as if it were said: "Is it farther than what I have witnessed of his excess in obeying desire and his obstinacy in turning away from following guidance, that you would compel him to belief, whether he wills or refuses?"

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 44:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand?﴾ is an *idrab* (a turning away from one subject to another) and a transition (*intiqal*) from the denial mentioned earlier to a denial of the Prophet's (ﷺ) supposing that they include anyone who hears or understands, as his (ﷺ) diligence in the call and his concern for guidance and admonition indicate. However, this is not on the basis that it does not occur, as the first (denial) does, but on the basis that it should not occur. That is: "Rather, do you suppose that most of them hear the verses that you recite to them, even to the extent of hearing, or understand the admonitions within them that restrain from ugly deeds and call to good ones, so that you care for their affair and hope for their faith?" The pronoun in "*akthara-hum*" (most of them) refers to *man* (those), and its plural is considered in light of its meaning, just as the singular forms of the earlier pronouns are considered in light of its wording. The pronoun in the two verbs refers to *akthar* (most), not to what it is attached to.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are only like cattle﴾ and so on, is a resumed clause (*jumla mustanafa*) brought to confirm the denial, to emphasize it, and to cut off the root of supposing altogether. That is: they are, in their failure to benefit from what strikes their ears of the thunderous verses, and in their lack of reflection upon the proofs and miracles they witness, nothing but like the beasts, which are a proverb for heedlessness and a sign for misguidance.

﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾ than them ﴿in way﴾, because cattle submit to their owner who feeds and looks after them; they recognize the one who does good to them from the one who harms them; they seek what benefits them and avoid what harms them; they find their way to their pastures and watering places and return to their stalls. These people, however, do not submit to their Lord, Creator and Provider; they do not recognize His kindness toward them from the harm of Satan, who is their most hostile enemy; they do not seek the reward, which is the greatest of benefits; they do not guard against the punishment, which is the most severe of harms and destructions; and they are not guided to the truth, which is the pleasant drinking place and the sweet, refreshing watering point. Moreover, if cattle do not hold a truth that leads to gaining good, they do not hold a falsehood that leads to committing evil; unlike these people, who have laid the foundations of falsehood and built upon them the rulings of evils. Further, the consequences of the cattle's ignorance and misguidance are confined to themselves, whereas the ignorance of these people leads to the outbreak of strife and corruption, the turning of people away from the path of rectitude, and the agitation of chaos and confusion among the servants. Furthermore, cattle do not leave any of the faculties deposited in them idle, but rather direct them toward what they were created for; so there is no failing on their part in seeking perfection. As for these people, they leave their intellectual faculties idle and waste the original natural disposition upon which people were created, and for this they deserve the greatest punishment and the most severe retribution.

(p-222) ﴿Have you not considered your Lord﴾ is an explanation of some of the proofs of *tawhid* (the oneness of God) following the explanation of the ignorance and misguidance of those who turn away from it. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the *hamza* is for confirmation (*taqrir*). Mentioning the attribute of lordship (*rububiyya*) with a pronominal suffix referring to him (ﷺ) is for his honor (ﷺ), and to indicate that what follows of the effects of His lordship and mercy, exalted is He. That is: Have you not looked at the wondrous creation of Him, exalted is He, ﴿how He extended the shadow﴾? That is: how He brought into being the shadow of whatever shade it was, whether from a mountain, a building, or a tree, at the beginning of sunrise, extended. This does not mean that He extended it after it had not been so, as it is after midday until sunset. For that, along with its lack of explicit statement that the shadow itself is by His creating and originating, is rejected by the context of the noble text. As for what has been said, that the shadow refers to what is between dawn and sunrise, and that it is the most pleasant of times, since pure darkness repels natures and the sun's rays heat the air and dazzle the sight, and for this reason the Garden was described with it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and an extended shade﴾, it is not sound. For there is no doubt that the purpose is to alert people to the great power of God, mighty and majestic, and to the far-reaching wisdom in what they witness. So the shadow must mean what they recognize as a specific state they witness in a place where a dense body comes between it and the sun, contrary to what is in its surroundings of the places where the sun shines. What was mentioned, though in reality it is a shadow of the eastern horizon, they do not count as a shadow, nor do they describe it with its familiar attributes. Perhaps directing the seeing to Him, glorified and exalted, although the purpose is affirming his (ﷺ) seeing of the manner of the extension of the shadow, is to alert that his (ﷺ) gaze is not confined to what it beholds of traces and workmanship; rather, the aim of his gazes is knowledge of the affairs of the Glorious Maker.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if He had willed, He would have made it still﴾ is a clause inserted between the two conjoined elements, to alert from the outset that there is no role in the extension mentioned for ordinary causes, and that the only effective factor is the will and power. The object of the will is omitted according to the established rule of its occurrence, and that its object is the content of the apodosis. That is: if He had willed its stillness, He would have made it still, i.e., fixed in its state of length and extension. He expressed this as stillness because its opposite, which is the change of its state according to changes in positions between the object casting it and the sun, is seen with the eye as motion and movement. The sum is that it does not undergo variation of state, in that the sun does not abrogate it. As for the explanation that He makes the sun stationary in one position, its basis is heedlessness of what the noble text is aimed at and expresses explicitly, namely the demonstration of His perfect, overpowering power and dazzling wisdom by attributing all originated matters directly to Him, exalted is He, and removing ordinary causes entirely from the rank of causality and influence, restricting them to mere indication of the existence of the effects. This is not done by mentioning His power over some extraordinary things, such as making the sun stand in one place, although that is greater than keeping the shadow in its state in indicating what was mentioned of perfect power and wisdom, since it is among its branches and consequences. So it is more worthy and more fitting to be presented in the context of explanation.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We made the sun for it a guide﴾ is conjoined to "extended" and falls under its ruling. That is: We made it a sign by whose changing states one is guided to its states, without there being between them any causality or influence in a definitive sense, as expressed by the inserted conditional clause. The turning to the plural of majesty ("We") is because in the said making, which is devoid of influence, along with the regular rotation observed between the sun and the shadow, which indicates causality, there is additional indication of the greatness of power and the subtlety of wisdom. This is the secret of using the word "then" (*thumma*), which indicates delay.

(p-223) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We drew it in﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) on "extended," which falls under its ruling. "Then" (thumma) indicates temporal sequence, since stating that the drawing-in and the extension are ordered and revolve around the axis of the benefits of created beings gives further indication of divine wisdom. It may also be taken to indicate sequence in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), meaning: We removed it after We had brought it into being extended, and We erased it by the sheer power and will of Ours at the moment the rays of the sun fell upon its place, without the sun having any influence in that at all. He expressed it by "drawing-in" (qabd), which indicates the entirety of what was spread out and its folding, since He had expressed its origination by "extension" (madd), which is spreading lengthwise. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to Us﴾ is to specify that its return is to Him, exalted is He, just as its origination is from Him, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿a easy drawing-in﴾ means: at a leisurely pace, little by little, according to the rising of its indicator (the sun), at a fixed, regular rate that brings about the benefits and conveniences of created beings. It has been said: when God, exalted is He, built the sky like a stretched dome and spread out the earth beneath it, the dome cast its shade upon the earth because there was no light-giver; and that is His extending it. Had He willed, He would have made it still and fixed in that state. Then He created the sun and set it over that shade, that is, He gave it authority over it and placed it as a guide that is followed, just as one follows a guide on the road; so the shade grows and shrinks with it, extends and contracts. Then He abrogated it by the sun and drew it in with an easy, smooth drawing-in, not a difficult one. It has also been said that this is a drawing-in that is easy at the Hour of Resurrection, by the withdrawal of its causes, namely the bodies that cast shadows; thus the annihilation of the shade is mentioned by the annihilation of its causes, just as its origination was mentioned by the origination of those causes. Describing it as easy follows the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That gathering is easy for Us﴾. The past tense form is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 47:

﴿It is He who made the night for you as a garment﴾ This is an explanation of some of the wondrous signs of His power and wisdom, and of the marvelous judgments of His mercy and His blessings that overflow upon creation, and of the variation of address so as to fulfill the station of bestowing favor its due. The lam is connected to "made" (ja'ala), and placing it before its two objects is for the sake of giving attention to the explanation that what follows it is of their benefit. In following the explanation of the states of the shade with the explanation of the rulings of the night, which is the shade of the earth, there is a subtlety of transition beyond which there is no further increase. That is to say: It is He who made the night for you like a garment, covering you with its darkness as a garment covers you.

﴿And the sleep as rest (subat)﴾ That is: and He made sleep, which occurs mostly at night, a cessation from the activities specific to the state of wakefulness. He expressed it with subat (rest/cessation), which is also death, because of the complete resemblance in the cessation of the rulings of life. To this point belongs His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back to Himself by night﴾, and His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep﴾.

﴿And He made the day a resurrection (nushur)﴾ That is: a time of being raised up from that rest, like the raising of the dead, by omitting the modifier and placing the modified in its position; or the raising itself, as an intensification. In this there is an indication that sleep and waking are a model of death and resurrection. And from Luqman, peace be upon him: "O my son, just as you sleep and are awakened, so you die and are raised."

"And it is He who sends the winds" (﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي أرْسَلَ الرِّياحَ﴾). It is also read in the singular (al-riyah, "the wind"), on the understanding that what is meant is the genus.

"As heralds" (﴿بُشْرًا﴾) is a lightened form of bushur, the plural of bashir (bushur, "glad tidings"), meaning: bearers of good tidings. It is also read bushran (بُشْرى) and nushran (نُشْرًا) with the nun, the plural of nashur, meaning: spreading out the clouds. It is also read with the lightened form and with a fatha on the nun, as a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description for the sake of emphasis.

His saying, exalted is He: "before His mercy" (﴿بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَحْمَتِهِ﴾) is a striking metaphor, meaning: in front of the rain.

The shift to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) in His saying, exalted is He: "And We send down from the sky pure water" (﴿وَأنْزَلْنا مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً طَهُورًا﴾) serves to display the utmost care in the sending down, because it is the result of what was mentioned of the sending of the winds. The meaning: We sent down, by Our majesty, through what We arranged of the sending of the winds, from the direction above, water that is eloquently pure. As for what has been said, that it is what is pure in itself and purifies others, that is an explanation of its eloquence in purity, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: "And He sends down upon you from the sky water to purify you" (﴿وَيُنَزِّلُ عَلَيْكم مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً لِيُطَهِّرَكُمْ﴾). In Arabic, tahur is either an adjective, as you say "pure water" (ماءٌ طَهُورٌ), or a noun, as in His saying (ﷺ): "Dust is the purifier of the believer" (﴿التُّرابُ طَهُورُ المُؤْمِنِ﴾). It has also come with the meaning of purification, as in your saying: "I purified myself with a good purification" (تَطَهَّرْتُ طَهُورًا حَسَنًا), like your saying "a good ablution" (وضُوءًا حَسَنًا). From it is His saying (ﷺ): "There is no prayer except with purification" (﴿لا صَلاةَ إلّا بِطَهُورٍ﴾). Describing water with it signals the completeness of the blessing in it, and a completion of the blessing in what follows, for pure water is more wholesome and more beneficial than water mixed with something that removes its purifying quality. It is also an alert that if their outward parts were to be purified, then their inner parts are more deserving and more fitting of that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 49:

﴿That We may give life thereby﴾, i.e., by means of what We sent down of water, the pure (ṭahūr) water, ﴿to a dead land﴾, by causing vegetation to grow. The masculine form (al-tadhkīr) is used because al-baldah is equivalent to al-balad, and also because it (maytan) does not follow the verb in its pattern, like the rest of the intensive patterns (abniyat al-mubālagha), so it is treated as a noun that is not derived (jāmid). What is meant by it is a piece of land, whether cultivated or uncultivated.

﴿And that We give drink to﴾, i.e., that pure water as it flows in the valleys, or as it gathers in the pools, the reservoirs or the wells.

﴿of what We have created, cattle and many humans﴾, i.e., the people of the desert who live by the rain. For this reason, al-an'ām (cattle) and al-anāsī (humans) are indefinite. Their being singled out for mention is because the people of towns and cities dwell near rivers and springs, so they, and the cattle they own, are independent of the water of the sky. The rest of the animals go far in seeking water, so drinking seldom fails them. Since the purpose of the noble verses, as it is for demonstrating the greatness of power, is here for enumerating the kinds of blessing, and since cattle, being a possession of humans whose general benefits and livelihoods depend on them, their watering is mentioned before the watering of humans, just as the revival of the land was mentioned before them, for it is the cause of their life and sustenance.

It is read as "nusqiyahu" (with a different vowelling), and asqā and saqā are two dialectal forms. It has been said that asqāhu means: he made for him a watering (suqyā). Al-anāsī is the plural of insī or insān, like ẓarābī in ẓarbān, on the basis that its original form was anāsīn, and its nūn was changed to yā'. It is also read anāsiya with lightening, by omitting the yā' of afā'īl, like anā'im in anā'īm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 50:

﴿And indeed We have repeated it﴾ That is: by Allah, We have indeed repeated this statement, which is the mention of the creation of the clouds and the sending down of rain, because of the beautiful aims mentioned in the Qur'an and in the other heavenly Books.

﴿among them﴾ That is: among the people, both the earlier and the later generations. ﴿that they may take heed﴾ that they may reflect, and thereby recognize the perfection of His power and the vastness of His mercy in this, and that they may rise to give thanks for His blessing as it truly deserves. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the rain, and that its being "distributed among them" means sending it down upon some lands and not others, or at some times and not others, or making it at one time a heavy downpour (wabil), at another a light drizzle (tall), at another a steady rain (dimah), and at another a fine mist (rahmah). The first interpretation is the most apparent.

﴿But most of the people refused﴾ of those who came before and after ﴿except disbelief﴾ That is: they did nothing but show ingratitude for the blessing and paid it little heed, or else denial of it, by saying, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-setting (nawʼ)," and not mentioning the making and mercy of Allah the Exalted. Whoever sees rain as coming only from the star-settings is a disbeliever, unlike one who holds that all of it is by the creation of Allah the Exalted. (p-225)

The star-settings (al-anwa') are signs for His making, may He be exalted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 51:

﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner (nadhir) to every town.﴾ (A prophet who would warn its people, so that the burdens of prophethood would be lighter upon you.) But We did not will that, so We did not do it; rather, We confined the matter to you, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds.﴾ This is in honor of you, in magnifying you, and in preferring you over all the messengers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 52:

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾. That is: meet that with steadfastness and diligent effort in the call (da'wah), in making the truth manifest, and in being firm with them. It is as if this were a prohibition to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ against showing leniency (mudara) toward them and gentleness (talattuf) in calling them, because he ﷺ used to desire that they enter Islam, and he would strive in that with the utmost effort by winning over their hearts (ta'lif qulubihim).

﴿And strive against them with it﴾. That is: with the Qur'an, by reciting what is within its passages of stern warnings (qawari'), admonitions (zawajir), and exhortations (mawa'iz), and by reminding them of the circumstances of the nations that denied their messengers.

﴿with a great striving﴾. For calling all the worlds in the manner mentioned is a great striving whose extent cannot be measured, in quantity and in quality. It has also been said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the abandonment of obedience (tark al-ta'ah), which is understood from the prohibition against obeying. But you should know that the mere abandonment of obedience is realized without any call at all, and it contains no trace of striving, let alone a great striving. Unless you make the "ba'" (bi-) indicate accompaniment (mulabasah), so that the meaning becomes: "and strive against them with what has been mentioned of the rulings of the noble Qur'an, accompanied by abandoning their obedience." It is as if it were said: "So strive against them with severity and harshness, not with conciliation and leniency," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾. The pronoun has also been taken to refer to what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town﴾, namely his ﷺ being a warner to all the towns. For if a warner had been sent to every town, it would have been obligatory upon each warner to strive against his own town, and all those struggles would have converged upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; thus his striving became great and magnificent on that account. So it was said to him ﷺ: "And strive against them, by virtue of your being a warner to all the towns, with a great striving that encompasses every act of striving." But you should know that explaining the cause of the greatness of the striving in terms of quantity adds no further benefit, since that was already stated explicitly; rather, what is fitting for the context is explaining the cause of its greatness and magnitude in terms of quality.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 53:

﴿And it is He who let loose the two seas﴾: that is, He left them side by side and adjoining, such that they do not mix, from "maraja dabbatahu" (he let his beast loose) when he left it free.

﴿This one is sweet and palatable﴾: quenching thirst, owing to its extreme sweetness. ﴿And this one is salty and bitter﴾: intensely salty. It is also read "malhun" (مَلْحٌ), which is perhaps a lightened form of "mālih," like "bard" for "bārid."

﴿And He made between them a barrier﴾: an invisible partition from His power, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾.

﴿And a forbidding ban﴾: an extreme repulsion, as if each of them seeks refuge from the other by that statement. It was also said: a limit that is set. This is like the Tigris, which enters the sea and cuts through it, flowing within it for parasangs without its taste changing. It was also said: what is meant by the sweet sea is the great river, by the salty sea the great ocean, and by the barrier the land between them. Then the effect of power is in the separation and the difference of attribute, even though the natural requirement of each element is cohesion, adhesion, and similarity in quality.

(p-226) ﴿And He it is who created man from water﴾. This is the water with which He kneaded the clay of Adam, peace be upon him, or He made it a component of the substance of humankind, so that it would gather together, become pliable, and be readied to receive forms and shapes with ease. Or it is the sperm-drop (nutfah).

﴿Then He made him into lineage and marriage-relation﴾. That is: He divided him into two kinds possessing lineage, namely males to whom descent is traced, and possessing marriage-relation, namely females with whom one enters into affinity, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He made from it the two spouses, the male and the female﴾.

﴿And your Lord is ever Competent﴾. Exaggerating in power, in that He is able to create from a single substance a human being with diverse limbs and widely differing natures, and to make him into two opposite kinds. Indeed, He may create from a single drop of sperm twins, a male and a female.

﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾ that, whose nature is what has been mentioned, ﴿what neither benefits them nor harms them﴾, i.e., that which by nature has no capacity for benefit or harm at all, and that is the idols. Or it means everything they worship besides Him, the Exalted, since no created being has independent power to benefit or harm.

﴿And the disbeliever is against his Lord﴾, whose signs of lordship have been mentioned, ﴿a helper﴾, backing Satan in enmity and in associating partners with Allah. By "the disbeliever" is meant the category (of disbelievers), or Abu Jahl. It has also been said that "ظَهِيرًا" (ẓahīran) here means "contemptible and despised," with no regard for him in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. This derives from their saying "ظَهَرْتُ بِهِ" (ẓahartu bihi), meaning "I cast him behind my back," when one discards something. Accordingly, it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah will neither speak to them nor look upon them﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 56:

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news﴾ to the believers, ﴿and a warner﴾ to the disbelievers.

Say, [O Muhammad], to them: "I do not ask you for any wage for it," meaning for conveying the message, which the sending (al-irsal) indicates, "from you," ﴿except for him who wills to take a way to his Lord﴾, meaning: except the act of one who wishes to draw near to Him, exalted is He, and seek nearness to Him through faith and obedience, in accordance with what I call you to. He has depicted that in the form of a wage, insofar as it is the intended object of the act. And he made an exception from it, cutting off entirely any admixture of greed, and showing the utmost compassion toward them, since he made that benefit, though it returns to them, return to him (ﷺ). It has also been said: the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so."

**And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die** — in seeking sufficiency against their evils and in being independent of their rewards, for He is the one truly deserving that one rely upon Him rather than the living whose lot is death; for when they die, whoever relied upon them is lost.

**And glorify Him with His praise** — He exalts Him above the attributes of deficiency, praising Him with the descriptions of perfection, seeking more of His bounty by giving thanks for His abundant blessings.

**And sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants** — whether apparent or hidden — **Acquainted** (khabīran), that is, having full awareness of them, such that nothing of them is concealed from Him, so He will recompense them with a complete recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 59:

﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾. Its interpretation has already passed. The place of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "who") is in the genitive case, as a further attribute of "the Living" (al-Hayy), who is described by an active attribute (al-sifah al-fi'liyyah) after being described by eternity (al-abadiyyah), which is among the essential attributes (al-sifat al-dhatiyyah). The reference to the attribute of all-encompassing knowledge serves to establish and emphasise the obligation of relying upon Him, may He be exalted. For whoever brought into being these great celestial bodies in this surpassing pattern and harmonious order, with firm arrangement and sound organisation, at specified times, while having complete power to create them all at once, for sublime wisdoms and beautiful ends that the intellects cannot fully grasp, is most worthy of being relied upon and most fitting to whom the matter is entrusted.

﴿Al-Rahman (the Most Merciful)﴾ is in the nominative case by way of praise (madh), meaning: He is the Most Merciful. In reality it is another attribute of "the Living." It was also read in the genitive case, which serves to further emphasise what was mentioned of the obligation of relying upon Him, may He be exalted, even though it does not follow the preceding word in i'rab (grammatical case). This is because it is established that the accusative and nominative forms used for praise, although they depart from following what precedes them in form, since they do not take its i'rab, are nonetheless called "cut off" (qat') for this reason; yet they are in truth followers of it. Do you not see how they obligated the omission of the verb and the subject in the accusative and nominative cases? This is to depict each of them in the form of a complement of what precedes it, and to draw attention to the intensity of the connection between them. The full verification was already discussed in the commentary on His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen...﴾, the verse. It has been said: the relative pronoun is the subject (mubtada') and "al-Rahman" is its predicate (khabar). It has also been said: "al-Rahman" is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun concealed in "istawa" (established).

﴿Ask about Him﴾, meaning: about the details of what was mentioned in summary of the creation and the establishment, not merely about the two themselves; for after their explanation there remains no need for asking, and there is no benefit in the transitive use with the preposition "bi" (about), since it is based on implying the meaning of "concern" (i'tina'), which requires that the thing asked about be a grave matter whose affair is of concern, not already possessed by the asker. It is evident that the creation and establishment themselves, after being mentioned, are not of this kind. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "If you doubt it, then ask about it an expert (khabir)," with the address directed to him (ﷺ) and the intended meaning being others, this is far from correct. Rather, the meaning is: if you wish to verify what was mentioned or to detail what was mentioned, then ask about it, seeking ﴿an expert﴾, great in standing, encompassing the outward and inward aspects of affairs, who is God, glory be to Him, who will inform you of the clear truth of the matter. It has also been said: ask about Him whoever has found Him in the earlier books, so that he may confirm to you concerning Him; and then there is no need for what we have mentioned. It has been said: the pronoun refers to "al-Rahman," and the meaning is: if they deny its application to God, may He be exalted, then ask about it those among the People of the Book who inform you, so that they may recognise the coming of what accompanies it in their books. On this view, it is permissible for "al-Rahman" to be the subject (mubtada') and what follows it the predicate (khabar). It is also read: "fa-sal" (ask).

﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ They said this either because they did not apply it (the name) to God Exalted, or because they thought that by it was meant someone other than God Exalted. For this reason they said: ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ That is, to the One you command us to prostrate to, or in response to your command to us, without knowing to whom the one to be prostrated to is. It was also said: it was because the word was *mu'arrab* (an Arabized word of foreign origin) and they had not heard it before. It was read as "*yamuruna*" with the *ya'* of the third person (يَأْمُرُنا), so that it is the statement of some of them to others.

﴿And it increased them﴾, that is, the command to prostrate to the Most Merciful, ﴿in aversion﴾ from faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 61:

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations (buruj)﴾. These are the twelve constellations (al-buruj al-ithna 'ashar), and they were named after this, since they are lofty palaces. The wandering planets (al-kawakib al-sayyara) reside in them as exalted dwellings for their inhabitants. The word is derived from al-burj (a tower), because of its prominence (zuhur).

﴿And placed in it a lamp (siraja)﴾. This is the sun, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And made the sun a lamp﴾ (71:16). It was read as "sarjan" (a variant reading, qira'ah), and it refers to the sun and the large stars (al-kawakib al-kibar) (p-228).

﴿And a luminous moon (qamaran muniran)﴾, shining at night. It was read as "qamaran," meaning "possessing a moon" (dhu qamar). It is the plural of qamra'. Since nights are described by the moon as moonlit (qamra'), the word was made into an idafa (construction of possession), then the first term was elided and its ruling was applied to the second term, which took its place, as in the verse of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

؎ Barada is splashed with the sealed, flowing wine ∗∗∗

That is, "the water of Barada" (the river Barada). It is also possible that the word carries the meaning of "moon," like al-rashad and al-rushd, and al-'arab and al-'urb.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 62:

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day alternating (khilfah)﴾ That is: possessors of alternation, each of them succeeding the other by taking its place in what one ought to do in it, or by the two alternating in turn, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾. And khilfah (alternation) is a noun for the state of one succeeding (khalafa), like rukbah (riding) and jilsah (sitting) from rakiba and jalasa.

﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾ That is: to remember the blessings of Allah, mighty and majestic, and to reflect upon the wonders of His handiwork, so that he knows that they must have a wise Creator, who is necessarily existent in His essence, merciful to His servants.

﴿or wishes to be grateful﴾ That is: to give thanks to Allah, exalted is He, for the bounties in them, or so that they become two times for those who remember: whoever misses his portion of litany (wird) in one of them makes it up in the other. And it has been read: "an yadhkura" (that he may remember), from dhakara, with the meaning of tadhakkara (remember).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 63:

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to explain the attributes of the sincere servants of the Most Merciful and their worldly and otherworldly conditions, after the explanation of the condition of those who shy away from worshipping Him and prostrating to Him. The idafa (genitive construction) is for honour (li-l-tashrif). It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is what follows it of the relative clause (al-mawsul) and what is conjoined to it. It has been said that it refers to the sentence beginning with the demonstrative at the end of the noble surah. It was also read as "ʿibādu l-Raḥmān," meaning: His accepted servants.

﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ means: with tranquillity and humility. "Hawnan" (in humility) is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptor, and its accusative case is either because it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "yamshūna" (they walk), or because it is an attribute (na't) of its verbal noun, meaning: they walk gently, soft-sided, without harshness, or a gentle walking.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and when the ignorant address them﴾ means: the foolish, as in the saying of one who said:

Surely none among us should act with ignorance against us,
lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant.

﴿they say, "Peace"﴾ is an explanation of their conduct in dealing with others, following the explanation of their condition within themselves. That is: when they are addressed with evil, they say a word of parting and disengagement (tasliman minkum wa-mutarakatan), "there is no good between us and you, no evil." It has been said: a sound word by which they keep away from harm and sin. There is no reference in it to their treatment of the disbelievers, such that it could be said that it was abrogated by the verse of fighting, as was related from Abu al-'Aliyah.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾ is an explanation of their condition in their dealings with their Lord, i.e., they are prostrating to their Lord and standing, that is, they spend the night in worship, all of it or part of it, through prayer. It has been said: "Whoever recites any portion of the Qur'an in prayer, even if it is little, has spent the night prostrating and standing." It has also been said: they refer to the two rak'ahs after Maghrib and the two rak'ahs after 'Isha'. The placing of prostration before standing is for the sake of preserving the rhyme of the verse-endings (fawasil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 65:

﴿And those who say﴾ i.e., at the conclusion of their prayers, or at all times in general, ﴿Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell, (p-229) for its punishment is ever-clinging﴾ i.e., a constant evil and an inescapable ruin. In this there is further praise of them, by explaining that they, despite their good dealings with creation and their striving in the worship of the Truth, fear the punishment and earnestly beseech God Most High to turn it away from them, differing in their deeds, like His saying, Most High: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will be returning to their Lord﴾.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 66:

﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and as a dwelling.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for their earlier request, mentioned above, based on the evil of its own condition, following the justification based on the evil condition of its punishment. It has been permitted that it be a justification for the first (clause), but that is not the case.

"Sa'at" (ساءَتْ) is in the sense of "ba'isat" (بَئِسَتْ, "it is wretched"), and within it there is an ambiguous pronoun (damir mubham) which is explained by "mustaqarran" (مُسْتَقَرًّا, "as a place of settlement"). The noun specified by the blame (al-makhsus bi-al-dhamm) is omitted, and its meaning is: "It is evil as a place of settlement and as a dwelling, it." This pronoun is what connects the sentence to the subject of "inna" (إنَّ) and makes it its predicate (khabar). It has been said: it is also permitted that "sa'at" be in the sense of "ahzanat" (أحْزَنَتْ, "it saddened"), with the pronoun of the subject of "inna" within it, and "mustaqarran" being a circumstantial accusative (hal) or a specifier (tamyiz); but this is remote, and it lacks the emphasis on describing the evil of its condition found in the first (reading). Likewise, making both justifications come from His side (the Exalted) is also (a view) of this kind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 67:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾: they did not exceed the bounds of generosity, ﴿nor were they niggardly﴾: nor did they constrict (their spending) with the constriction of the miser. It was also said: extravagance (israf) is spending on acts of disobedience, and niggardliness (qatr) is withholding obligatory duties and acts of nearness (to God). It is also read with a kasra on the ta' and a fatha on the ya' (yaqturu, i.e. yaqtiru), and with a kasra on it lightened and doubled with a damma on the ya' (yuqtiru).

﴿And was between that﴾: that is, between what was mentioned of extravagance and niggardliness, ﴿a standard (qawaman)﴾: a middle course and a balance. It was named thus because both extremes are upright, just as the word sawa' (equal) was used for it because both extremes are equal. It is also read with a kasra (qiwaman), and it means what the need is met with, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It is a second predicate, or a confirming circumstantial clause (hal), or it is the predicate and "between that" is a superfluous element (laghw). It has also been permitted that it be the subject of kana, on the basis that it is indeclinable because it is attached to a non-declinable word; but its weakness is not hidden, for it carries the meaning of qiwam, so it would be like giving information about a thing concerning itself.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 68:

﴿And those who do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. This begins an explanation of their abstention from sins after the explanation of their performance of acts of obedience. The mention of the negation of extravagance (israf) and niggardliness (qatr) serves to realize the meaning of moderation (iqtisad). The explicit description of them by the negation of associating partners with Allah, despite the evidence of their faith, serves to show the utmost care for monotheism (tawhid) and sincerity (ikhlas), and to magnify the matter of killing and fornication by placing them in the same series. It also contains an allusion to what the disbelievers among the Quraysh and others were upon. That is: they do not worship another god along with Him, exalted is He.

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾. That is: He has forbidden it, meaning: He has forbidden its killing. The genitive noun (al-mudaf) has been elided and the genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayhi) put in its place, for the sake of emphasis on the prohibition.

﴿except with right﴾. That is: they do not kill it for any reason except for a reason of right (al-haqq) that removes its sanctity and inviolability; or: they do not commit any killing except one connected with right; or: they do not kill it in any state except while being connected with right.

﴿And they do not commit fornication﴾. That is: those who do not do any of these grave, ugly deeds, which the disbelievers combined, since they, along with their associating partners with Him, glorified be He, were persistent in killing forbidden souls, among which is the buried infant girl (al-mawuda), and were devoted to fornication, not refraining from it at all.

﴿And whoever does that﴾. That is: what has been mentioned, as is the custom of the disbelievers (p-230) mentioned, ﴿shall meet﴾ in the Hereafter. It was also read "yalaqqa" with doubling, jussive, ﴿a sin (athama)﴾. It is the recompense of sin, like "wabal" and "nakal" in form and meaning. It was said: it is sin itself, that is: he shall meet the recompense of sin. The tanwin (nunation) in both interpretations is for emphasis (tafkhim). It was also read "ayyaman", that is: severe days (shada'id). It is said: "yawm dhu ayyam" for a difficult day.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 69:

﴿Its punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "yalqa" (he will meet), because the two are identical in meaning, like the saying of the poet:

"Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood, well-cut, and a fire blazing."

It was also read in the nominative (marfu') as a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) or in the circumstantial sense (hal), and likewise what is conjoined to it. It was also read: "yudha'af" and "nudha'if lahu al-'adhab" with the nun and the accusative on "al-'adhab."

﴿And he will abide therein﴾, that is, in that doubled punishment, ﴿humiliated﴾, abased, despised, combining bodily and spiritual torment. It was also read: "yukhlad" and "yukhallad", in the passive voice, from al-ikhlad (to make to abide) and al-takhlid (to cause to abide).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 70:

It is also read "takhludu" with the ta' (taa'), by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, from the third person to the second), which indicates the intensity of wrath and the multiplication of punishment, since sins are added to disbelief, as is made clear by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾. The mention of the described (al-mawsuf) together with the use of "al-salih" and "al-salihat" functioning as a proper noun (majra al-ism) serves to draw attention to it and to specify its distinctness from the former deeds.

﴿Then those﴾: a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), and the plural is used in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular is used in the three verbs in consideration of its wording; that is, "those who are described with repentance, faith, and righteous deeds." ﴿Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾: by erasing the prior sins through repentance and establishing in their place the subsequent acts of obedience; or by replacing the disposition toward disobedience and its inclinations in the soul with the disposition of obedience, by removing the former and bringing the latter. It has been said: by Him granting them success in the opposites of what preceded from them; or by establishing for each punishment a reward in its place. It has also been said: He will replace for them shirk with faith, the killing of Muslims with the killing of polytheists, and fornication with chastity and wedlock.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾: a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiradh tadhyili) that confirms what preceded it of erasure and establishment.

Translation:

﴿And whoever repents﴾, i.e., turns away from sins by abandoning them entirely and feeling remorse for them, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, by which he makes up for what he has neglected or departed from sins, and enters into acts of obedience.

﴿Then indeed he﴾, by what he has done, ﴿turns back to Allah﴾, i.e., returns to Him, exalted is He, ﴿with a [sincere] turning﴾, i.e., a turning of great stature, well-pleasing in His sight, erasing punishment and securing reward; or [it means] he turns with a turning to Allah, exalted is He, who loves those who turn back (al-tawwabin) and shows kindness to them; or [it means] indeed he returns to Him, exalted is He, or to His reward, with a good return. This is a generalization after a specification.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 72:

﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood﴾ — that is, they do not give false testimony, or they do not attend gatherings of falsehood, for being present at falsehood is a form of participating in it.

﴿And when they pass by idle talk﴾ — by chance — ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾. That is, what is idle (al-laghw, i.e., that which ought to be discarded and cast aside, being devoid of any good) — ﴿they pass by with dignity﴾, turning away from it and honoring themselves by not standing over it or plunging into it. Among this is overlooking indecencies, pardoning sins, and using allusion for what is shameful to state explicitly.

(p-231) ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord﴾ containing admonitions and rulings, ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾. That is, they throw themselves upon them, listening with attentive ears and regarding them with watchful eyes. He expressed this by negating the opposite, as an allusion to the conduct of the disbelievers and hypocrites. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the vain things (al-laghw) that are implied by the mention of idle talk.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 74:

﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the coolness of the eyes"﴾, by their being granted success in obedience and in acquiring virtues. When a believer is supported by his family in obeying God, Mighty and Majestic, and they share in it with him, his heart is gladdened by them and his eye is cooled by them, because of what he witnesses of their following him in the paths of the religion, and his expectation that they will join him in Paradise, as He promised in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall join their offspring to them﴾. The "min" (من) here is either for the beginning of the extent (ibtida'iyya) or explanatory (bayaniyya). It has been read as "wa-dhurriyyatā" (وذُرِّيَتا). The indefiniteness of "a'yun" (أعين, "eyes") is intended to make "qurra" (قرة, "coolness") indefinite, for magnification, and its paucity is intended, because what is meant is the eyes of the God-fearing, and there is no doubt about their scarcity compared with others.

﴿And make us a leader for the God-fearing﴾, that is: make us such that they will follow us in establishing the religion's observances, by the outpouring of knowledge and the granting of success in action. The singular "imam" (إمامًا) is used to indicate the category and to avoid confusion, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾. Or it is because what is meant is: make each one of us a leader. Or it is because they are like a single soul, owing to the unity of their path and the agreement of their word. Thus they have said. But you should know that the whole matter rests on this supplication being uttered either by all of them together, in the manner of accompaniment (al-ma'iyya), and that is impossible, since their gathering in a single age is impossible, so what do you suppose about their gathering in a single assembly and their agreeing upon a single word? Or it is uttered by each one of them separately, with the others being included in the request for leadership, and that is not definitely established. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is depicted from them in the form of individual utterance, and that the wording of each one of them in the supplication was: "And make me a leader for the God-fearing." Except that the wordings of all of them have been reported in the first-person plural form, for the purpose of brevity, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, and "imaman" (إمامًا) was left in its own form. It has also been said: "al-imam" is the plural of "amm" (آمّ), meaning "one who intends," like "siyam" as the plural of "sa'im." Its meaning is: intending them, following them. The repetition of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, الموصول) in the seven positions, while the mention of the predicates by way of coordination with the predicate of the first relative pronoun would have sufficed, is to signify that each of the things mentioned within the scope of the predicate of the aforementioned relative pronouns is a distinguished attribute in its own right, having a grave importance, and deserving to be assigned a separate, independent subject, and that none of it should be made a complement of something else. The placement of the conjunction between the relative pronouns serves to render the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence, as in his saying:

*To the mighty king and the son of the hero,*
*and the lion of the battalions in the crowd.*

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 75:

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (Those) is a demonstrative referring to those characterized by what was distinguished in the relative clause of the eight relative pronouns (al-mawsulat al-thamaniyah), in respect of their being characterized by it. It indicates that they are distinguished by that to the utmost degree of distinction, being arranged by means of it in the row of visibly observed matters. The sense of distance in it serves to announce the remoteness of their rank in excellence. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They will be rewarded with the lofty chamber (al-ghurfah)﴾. The sentence is resumptive (mustaanifah), having no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case position), explaining what they have in the Hereafter of everlasting happiness following the explanation of what they have in this world of excellent deeds.

Al-ghurfah: the high degree among dwellings, and every elevated, lofty building. That is, they will be recompensed with the highest dwellings of Paradise. It is a noun of genus (ism jins) intended in the plural, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be secure in the lofty chambers﴾. It has also been said that it is one of the names of Paradise.

﴿Bima sabaru﴾ (because of their patience), that is, by their patience in hardships, from the bitterness of acts of obedience, the renunciation of desires, and the bearing of struggles. ﴿And they will be met therein﴾ from the direction of the angels ﴿with greeting and peace﴾. That is, the angels will greet them and pray for them with long life and safety from calamities; or they will be given permanence and eternity together with safety from every calamity. It has also been said: some of them will greet others and salute them. And it has been read: "yalqawna" from laqiya.

"Abiding therein forever" (khalidina fiha): they do not die, nor are they taken out. "Excellent as a place of settlement and abode" (hasunat mustaqarran wa muqama): the discussion of this is like that which has passed concerning its counterpart.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 25, verse 77:

﴿Say﴾ The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to make clear to the people that those who triumph with that magnificent blessing, for which competitors vie, have attained it only through the virtues just enumerated, and that without them they would not be counted at all. That is: say to them all, addressing them directly, with regard to what has proceeded from their kind of good and evil: ﴿My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾. That is: what weight would your Lord give to you, and what regard would be shown to you, were it not for your worship of Him, the Exalted, as its detailed explanation has passed. For man was created for the purpose of knowing Him, the Exalted, and obeying Him; otherwise he and the rest of the beasts are equal. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "What weight would you have in His sight?" It was also said: its meaning is, "What would my Lord do with you were it not for His calling you to Islam?" And it was said: its meaning is, "What would He do with your punishment were it not for your calling upon others alongside Him as gods?" It is also permissible for "ma" to be negative, and His statement, the Exalted, ﴿For you have denied﴾ is an explanation of the state of the disbelievers among those addressed, just as what precedes it is an explanation of the state of the believers among them. That is: you have denied what I informed you of and opposed it, O disbelievers, and you did not act as those mentioned did. It was also said: "you have fallen short in worship," from the expression "kadhaba al-qitalu" when fighting is not carried out with full effort. It was also read: "For those who disbelieve have denied," that is, the disbelievers among you, since the address is general to both groups; and its purpose is to signal that the criterion for the triumph of one group and the loss of the other, despite the shared kind that makes their sharing in the triumph valid, is nothing but their difference in deeds.

﴿So it will be a binding punishment﴾ That is: the consequence or effect of denial will be a necessary outcome that will befall you without doubt, until it casts you face-down into the Fire, as the particle "fa" indicates, signifying the necessity of what follows for what precedes. It is left unmentioned to signal how plainly evident it is and to convey the magnitude of its affair, and to alert that it is something that explanation cannot encompass. It was also said: the punishment will be binding (lizaman). It is reported from Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, that it is the killing on the day of Badr, and that it was made binding among the slain. It was also read "lazaman" with a fatha, meaning "necessity," like "thabat" and "thubut" (steadfastness and firmness).

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Furqan will meet Allah, the Exalted, while he is a believer that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and he will be admitted to Paradise without toil."
